A 58-year-old man, who after reporting several days of abdominal pain was found to have acute kidney injury, was transferred to our unit from a regional hospital.In the preceding 6 months, the patient had been diagnosed with frontotemporal dementia; he had no personal or family history of nephrolithiasis, bowel disease, or weight loss. Notably, the year before this presentation, his kidney function had been found to be normal with the serum creatinine concentration recorded as 71 μmol/L (normal range 60–115).
On examination, the patient was clinically well with a blood pressure of 122/66 mm Hg, heart rate of 95 beats per min, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, and an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air.
Laboratory investigations confirmed acute kidney injury—his serum creatinine concentration was 703 μmol/L with preserved urinary output; his remaining serum biochemistry was unremarkable. The urinary protein/creatinine ratio was 39 mg/mmol (normal range 0–12·5).
The patient was admitted to the nephrology ward for a kidney biopsy which showed acute tubular injury with abundant intratubular calcium oxalate crystals; the background kidney was healthy, with little scarring, and only 1/14 obsolete glomeruli (figure).
A detailed dietary history found that the patient had been eating 500–1000 g of almonds daily over the last four years—corresponding to approximately 2–4 g of oxalate per day. He had no evidence of malabsorption; his faecal elastase concentration was >500 ug/g (typical range 200 to less than 500).
A CT of the kidney, ureter, and bladder showed a non-obstructing 1·4 cm calculus in the lower pole of the right kidney and a non-obstructing 0·6 cm calculus in the distal left ureter (figure). We concluded the patient had a diet-related secondary hyperoxaluria; frontotemporal dementia is associated with unusual, compulsive eating habits.
As he was asymptomatic, we decided to manage him conservatively; the patient was started on a low-oxalate, high-calcium diet with a high fluid intake and reviewed regularly. At his last appointment, the patient's laboratory results showed his serum creatinine concentration was improving (478 μmol/L).
Hyperoxaluria causes calcium oxalate stones by raising urinary saturation of calcium oxalate; hyperoxaluria can result from ingestion of oxalate-rich foods, such as rhubarb, spinach, beetroot, almonds—as in our case—and chocolate. Hyperoxaluria is less common than hypercalciuria as a cause of calcium oxalate stones.
Non-obstructive kidney stones of less than 15 mm can be treated conservatively and monitored closely; an increase in the size of the stone or complications, such as infections, may result in a more proactive approach.
options: Faecal microbiome testing, Genetic testing, Dietary history, Faecal elastase

A 53-year-old man presented to the emergency department of our hospital in January, 2014, after a syncopal episode. He was a regular smoker and recreational drug user, and had taken heroin, cannabis, and benzodiazepine during that week. He had a history of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. On examination he had grey pallor and was dyspnoeic at rest (respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute). His oxygen saturation was 70% on 100% inspired oxygen and his blood sample, which showed anaemia (haemoglobin 54 g/L; normal 130–180 g/L), was chocolate brown (figure). Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7·40 (7·35–7·45) and methaemoglobin 26% (<2%).
Oxidant agents like benzocaine or novocaine, which are sometimes added to street heroin and cocaine, oxidise haemoglobin from its ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric state (Fe3+), and can cause methaemoglobinaemia. This altered form of haemoglobin loses its ability to transport oxygen, and can cause hypoxaemia. Chocolate-coloured blood is typical of methaemoglobinaemia. Unlike deoxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin does not brighten on exposure to atmospheric oxygen. In our patient, haemolysis associated with G6PD deficiency caused release of the methaemoglobin from within the red blood cells into the serum.
options: Thalassemia, Methemoglobinemia, Drepanocytosis, Carbon monoxide poisoning

input:
A 58-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 10-h history of acute lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient was otherwise healthy with no significant medical history.On examination, she had generalised, mild abdominal tenderness especially in the left lower quadrant where there was guarding and rebound tenderness; her vital signs were normal—blood pressure 127/66 mm Hg, temperature 37·3 oC, heart rate of 59 beats per min, and respiratory rate was 12 breaths per min.
Blood tests showed elevated white blood cell count of 12·4 × 109 per mL and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 22 mg/L. An abdominal CT confirmed a diagnosis of acute left-sided colonic diverticulitis and showed intraperitoneal free air.
We decided to manage the case conservatively, and gave the patient intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam (4 g and 0·5 g) three times a day; she was also allowed a light diet. After an initial increase in serum CRP concentration, there followed a decline: 22 mg/L to 190 mg/L to 300 mg/L to 250 mg/L to 180 mg/L; the decrease was accompanied by an improvement in the patient's clinical state. She was allowed home after 5 days in the hospital and the intravenous antibiotics were switched to oral; she went on to make an event-free recovery. At routine colonoscopy, 3 months later, there were no signs of malignancy.
Left-sided colonic diverticulosis is common in western countries. The lifetime risk for acute diverticulitis is approximately 5–25% in patients with diverticulosis. CT has become the gold standard method of diagnosing diverticulitis and its complications; distant free air is a radiological sign of a free perforation.
Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis has a mild natural course and is usually managed without antibiotics. In cases of sepsis, immunosuppression, or CT-proven complications—the presence of abscesses or extraluminal air—antibiotics are indicated. Perforation with generalised peritonitis—as seen in our case—is associated with high morbidity and mortality—and traditionally, free air alone was an indication for laparotomy with resection of the affected colon segment and end-colostomy. However, in recent years, the trend has been towards a more conservative approach; the latest evidence shows that such a move has resulted in fewer patients requiring a stoma. Further, many immunocompetent, haemodynamically stable patients with acute perforated diverticulitis and extraluminal air can be treated conservatively especially if there is only pericolic air. Immediate surgery is indicated in septic patients and if there are clinical signs of generalised peritonitis or treatment failure. Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage without resection is safe in selected patients with purulent peritonitis; alternatively, resection is recommended—and, depending on the patient's condition, a primary anastomosis or an end colostomy should be performed (video).
output: Conservative treatment with antibiotics and close observation
target: Conservative treatment with antibiotics and close observation

A 47-year-old woman presented to our clinic with a 1-month history of a painful, itching, non-healing, and oozing lesion on the left side of her neck (figure). In addition to the lesion, she reported having disturbed sleep because of pain and pruritus in the affected area. The problem developed between 4 and 5 weeks after a trip to the Mediterranean coast of southern Turkey. An oral antibiotic and iodine ointment had failed to make any improvement.On clinical examination, the lesion was a single ulcer with yellow exudate and an indurated erythematous margin. The patient also had palpable, indolent lymphadenopathy of the submental lymph nodes. A bacterial swab showed coagulase-negative staphylococci. Initially, we suspected that the patient might have cutaneous leishmaniasis and we took two punch biopsy samples from both the centre and margin of the lesion for PCR and histological analyses. Haematoxylin and eosin staining of the central biopsy showed plasma-cell-rich granulation tissue. Immunohistochemical staining for Treponema pallidum showed spirochetes (figure). Laboratory test results showed a positive non-treponemal venereal disease research laboratory test titre of 1:8, as well as positive specific assays—the T pallidum particle agglutination assay, IgM immunoblot, and IgG ELISA. On further inquiry, the patient explained that she had unprotected sexual intercourse during her holiday. She reported that her partner had wounds on the lips that may have been the source of infection. A diagnosis of a primary syphilitic chancre was made, and the patient was treated with benzylpenicillin at 2 400 000 IU, intramuscularly. The ulceration resolved 3 weeks after treatment.
Primary syphilis usually consists of a single, painless, non-itching, sharply bordered ulceration—called a chancre—with regional lymphadenopathy. Syphilitic chancres can show great clinical variability: less than 10% are extragenital occurring in any location. Most of these cases have been described on the abdomen, breasts, fingers, and in and around the mouth. A syphilitic chancre should, therefore, be a diagnostic consideration—albeit in some places an unlikely possibility—in any non-healing, indurated ulcer found anywhere on the body.

options: Squamous cell carcinoma, Cutaneous leishmaniasis, Extra-genital syphilitic chancre, Scrofuloderma

A 59-year-old woman was admitted to our emergency department for asthenia and swollen ankles. 1 week earlier she began to feel tired while walking. On clinical examination, we found peripheral oedema but no other signs suggestive of heart failure. Her blood pressure was 150/70 mm Hg. An electrocardiogram showed junctional bradycardia (35 beats per min): P waves were absent and the QRS complexes were regular and narrow. In her medical history, it was noted that she had recently been treated with ibuprofen and colchicine for acute idiopathic pericarditis: the patient had chest pain and paroxysmal atrial flutter. After this episode she had travelled to the Philippines and had further cardiac problems so was started on digoxin 0·25 mg/day.Our laboratory investigations showed a high digoxin concentration (3·97 ng/mL) and a raised concentration of C-reactive protein (12 mg/L) in her serum. An autoimmune antibody screen was negative and microbiology tests—including serum antibodies for hepatitis A, B, and C, and HIV, QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube test and urine PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Aspergillus fumigatus serum antigen, and blood cultures for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria—were not positive. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a severe pericardial effusion with thickening of the myocardium on the roof of the right atrium suggestive of a cardiac mass. An MRI also confirmed an effusion causing cardiac tamponade (figure). We stopped the digoxin and the patient's condition improved immediately. We also did a pericardiocentesis, which drained 800 mL of serous fluid—also negative on microbiological tests and showed no malignant cells. The cardiac MRI was repeated, and the images showed a thickening of the right atrial roof, interatrial septum, and atrioventricular sulcus. Further investigations—which did not show any metastatic neoplasia—were key in steering us towards a diagnosis of a multisystem disorder—namely, Erdheim–Chester disease. A CT scan and MRI of the abdomen showed bilateral dilatation of the renal pelvises and retroperitoneal fibrosis—known as hairy kidneys. Additionally, the MRI showed periadventitial thickening of the abdominal aorta—yet another pathognomonic sign of Erdheim–Chester disease—known as coated aorta. An endomyocardial biopsy specimen provided histological evidence of the diagnosis, showing an infiltration with non-Langerhans histiocytes: immunohistochemical analysis was positive for CD68 but negative for CD1a and S100. We also found the patient had a mutation of the BRAF gene, specifically BRAFV600E. Soon after admission she became lethargic and confused, so we did an MRI of her brain, which showed a parenchymal lesion of the left trigone of the lateral ventricle. Our patient died 4 weeks after admission.
Erdheim–Chester disease, a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, is a rare multisystem disorder of adulthood. It is characterised by excessive production and accumulation of histiocytes in multiple tissues and organs. Prognosis is poor—especially when the heart and brain are affected. Diagnosis is challenging and should be suspected in the presence of indicators of a multisystem disease.
options: Beck, Kussmaul, Broadbent, Erdheim–Chester

input: An 80-year-old woman was referred to the Chitose City Hospital (Chitose, Japan) with a 6 month history of a slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. She had been attending dialysis three-times a week for 10 years for chronic renal failure. A laboratory assessment showed the following abnormalities: serum calcium of 1·95 mmol/L (normal range 2·05–2·55), serum phosphorus of 3·3 mmol/L (0·74–1·52 mmol/L), serum intact parathyroid hormone of 142 ng/L (10–65 ng/L), and serum creatinine of 787 μmol/L (53–106 μmol/L). She was poorly compliant with taking phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical examination showed a firm, irregularly shaped, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in the major axis on her right lumbar area (figure, A). CT scans showed a lobular calcified mass with fibrous capsules in the subcutis (figure, B, C). 67Ga-scintigram showed an abnormal gallium accumulation corresponding to the right lumbar mass, with no other pathological uptake (figure, D). After a diagnosis of secondary tumoral calcinosis was made, the patient was managed by use of a phosphate-restricted diet, phosphate-binding medication, and an intensifying dialysis programme, which aimed to reduce the serum concentration of calcium–phosphorus products.
options: Tumoral calcinosis, Calcifying epithelioma, Osteosarcoma, Sarcoidosis

A 34-year-old man was brought to our Emergency Department after a truck ran over the right side of his body while he was out walking. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient's vital signs were stable; he had tenderness over his right shoulder, mild tenderness and bruising over the right hip, and abrasions over the right side of his arm, chest, abdomen, and right flank. His pelvis was stable, and movements of the right hip joint were unaffected.
Laboratory investigations were within normal range. No fractures were seen on x-rays of the patient's chest, pelvis, right shoulder, and right femur. A whole-body CT scan showed subcutaneous haematomas about 3·5 cm × 3·0 cm in the right infra-axillary region, right lateral abdominal wall, and pelvis.
We admitted the patient under the trauma service; an MRI of his right shoulder showed an acute contusion of the right supraspinatus muscle and right acromioclavicular joint. The patient was allowed home after an orthopaedic review with a plan of conservative treatment: analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy.
At follow-up with his general practitioner, 3 weeks later, the patient had an ill-defined soft, fluctuant swelling over his right flank and a fluctuant, non-tender swelling around the right hip with no abnormalities of the overlying skin.
At further assessment, 5 weeks after the accident, the swelling over the patient's right flank had resolved, but the one over his right hip area had grown larger. An MRI of the right hip showed a large 14 cm × 9·5 cm × 26 cm fluid signal collection with multiple fat locules within the deep subcutaneous tissue of the right posterolateral proximal thigh and hip, immediately superficial to the intact deep fascia (figure). The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of a Morel-Lavallée lesion.
The patient underwent open debridement; a mixture of blood and serous fluid was drained from the lesion and multiple pseudo-polyps, that had formed as a result of fat necrosis, were excised along with the capsule of the cavity. The cavity was washed out and the incision was closed.
The patient was allowed home. At postoperative follow-up in the trauma clinic, 4 weeks later, the lesion had completely resolved.
A Morel-Lavallée lesion is a rare, closed, internal degloving soft-tissue injury usually resulting from trauma. Lesions can present acutely after the trauma or they can develop a few days or weeks after the injury; they are often missed initially—as in our case. They develop by shearing forces which lead to separation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues from the underlying fascia, leading to fluid accumulation in the perifascial space.
In approximately 8% of cases, Morel-Lavallée lesions are associated with underlying pelvic or acetabular fractures—although the true incidence may be higher in such patients. When the lesion is small, it may be overlooked. Additionally, Morel-Lavallée lesions are sometimes misdiagnosed as a post-traumatic muscle contusion, haematomas, or myositis ossificans. Early recognition of the condition prevents the development of complications such as infections or skin necrosis. MRI is the investigation of choice, aiding diagnosis, and guiding management.
options: Haematoma, Post-traumatic myositis ossificans, Morel-Lavallée lesion, Neoplasm

input:
A 62-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a dark, atypical-looking lesion on his upper arm because the medical oncologists were concerned that it was possibly an early melanoma (appendix).The patient was otherwise fit and well; he had a malignant melanoma surgically removed from the middle of his back 18 months previously. He reported a history of renal cell carcinoma treated by a partial nephrectomy.
The lesion was examined using reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) and showed a large, nucleated, solitary cell consistent with a Langerhans cell in the upper epidermis with a round or oval cell body, measuring approximately 20 μm, and highly refractile dendritic branches (figure).
Histology of the lesion confirmed a lentiginous junctional nevus with inflammation: a benign diagnosis.
RCM is an in vivo optical imaging technique used to visualise skin cells, appendages, and processes in real time; the technology allows for subcellular resolution in the horizonal or en face orientation of skin layers down to the papillary dermis showing superficial collagen. RCM uses a low-power, near-infrared, diode laser, emitting light of wavelength 820 nm.
Crucially, RCM cannot distinguish between activated Langerhans cells and dendritic melanocytes. Both have similar refractive indices and morphological features. However, their distribution is different and—as in our patient—a Langerhans cell might be suspected due to its location.
Since RCM is a newer diagnostic imaging approach being used more commonly now than ever before, it is useful to have some awareness of potential pitfalls when interpreting confocal images and identifying cells of interest.
Finally, Langerhans cells may become activated in the context of inflammatory immune response or trauma. While the transformation rate of a melanocytic nevus into cutaneous melanoma is thought to be extremely low—about 1 in 33 000 for men older than 60 years—it remains important to examine and remove suspicious lesions as rates of cutaneous melanoma continue to rise (video).
options: Dermoscopy, Optical coherence tomography, Ultrasound, Reflectance confocal microscopy

input:
A girl aged 13 years presented with mild subcutaneous vertex tumefaction and localised alopecia (figure A). She was administered bisphosphonate and infliximab for SAPHO syndrome (ie, synovitis, acnea conglobata, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis), diagnosed 2 years earlier on the basis of multifocal osteitis (ie, long bones metaphysis, pelvis and costal bones, and a vertebra; figure B) and a papulopustular palmar rash. Initial bone biopsy had shown no malignancy, with a positive culture for Propionibacterium acnes—a frequent finding in people with SAPHO syndrome.
During the next 4 months, the scalp lesions gradually evolved to large, subcutaneous, painful nodules with purulent discharge, skin thickening, and expanding alopecia (figure C). This progression was contemporary with a change from infliximab to tofacitinib because of drug intolerance. Further investigations showed moderate inflammatory syndrome (C-reactive protein 47·8 mg/L [reference value <1·0 mg/L]; neutrophils 14·3 × 109/L [reference value 1·8–7·0 × 109/L]) and multiple active osteitis foci. Tofacitinib was discontinued while waiting for the infectious test and was not started again. Microbial sampling (biopsy and swab) of the scalp abscesses returned negative on two occasions, including specific mycobacterium and fungus cultures. Biopsy showed deep-seated neutrophilic abscess, follicular inflammation and destruction, and dermal fibrosis (figure D, E) and sequencing of a gene panel associated with inborn errors of immunity (eg, IL1RN and PSTPIP1) reported no pathogenic variants.
A diagnosis of dissecting cellulitis of the scalp was made. After failure of potent topical steroids, the patient was started on isotretinoin and a course of systemic steroids (prednisolone 0·5 mg/kg, weaned during 8 months). After 1 year of follow-up, osteitis remains mildly active but subcutaneous collections and alopecia area have substantially reduced under ongoing bisphosphonate and isotretinoin therapy (appendix).
Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp belongs to the spectrum of follicular occlusion syndrome (alongside acnea conglobata and hidradenitis suppurativa), a grouping of neutrophilic inflammatory skin diseases manifesting with sterile nodules, abscesses, and scarring. Although acnea conglobata and hidradenitis suppurativa are relatively frequent findings in people with SAPHO syndrome, dissecting cellulitis of the scalp has been rarely reported in this syndrome. This Clinical Picture aims to increase awareness and early recognition of this uncommon manifestation of SAPHO syndrome, as timely therapy can improve outcomes. Further research is needed to define optimal therapy of simultaneous bone and skin inflammation in people with SAPHO syndrome after non-response to anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy (ie, anti-IL-17 or anti-IL-23).

A 4-year-old boy was brought to our hospital with an 18-month history of progressive swelling in his neck. His parents said that over the previous few months he had begun to snore. Before he was seen by us he had been treated empirically at another hospital for extra-pulmonary tuberculosis without any improvement of his symptoms.On examination he had widespread lymphadenopathy, most markedly in the neck and axilla (figure); the nodes in the neck were suppurative. He had hepatosplenomegaly but was not malnourished. Our initial differential diagnosis was tuberculosis, filariasis, or lymphoma. Blood tests showed the boy to be anaemic, with a haemoglobin concentration of 7·3 g/dL. He had a raised platelet count (1000 × 109 per L), a significantly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and raised lactate-dehydrogenase levels. Blood cultures and an HIV test were negative. We did a lymph node biopsy, bone marrow aspiration, and CT scan of his head and neck. The lymph node biopsy result showed granulomatous infiltration with negative infective stains and the bone marrow was normal. A CT scan of the boy's head showed widespread lymphadenopathy, and a lytic lesion in the skull (figure). Considering all the information together, we made a provisional diagnosis of a histiocytic disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH); the degree of lymphadenopathy was phenotypically consistent with Rosai-Dorfman-Destombes (RDD) disease. Full histological analysis, including immunological staining, was not available in Kenya; however, our local expert's opinion was that the pathology was consistent with the provisional diagnosis. So due to the severity and duration of the patient's symptoms, he was started on treatment with prednisone 40 mg/m2 daily for 4 weeks, tapered over 2 weeks, and vinblastine 6 mg/m2 per week for 6 weeks.
Happily, over the next 6 months, the boy's symptoms dramatically improved on continuation therapy: vinblastine, prednisone, and mercaptopurine (figure). We will continue treatment until he has completed a total of 52 weeks of chemotherapy.
In the process of reviewing the case for publication in The Lancet, the histology was examined by an expert in France, who confirmed that our patient did indeed have a rare form of mixed type histiocytosis—LCH and RDD. All the boy's histocytes strongly expressed S100, with around 30% of these cells also expressing CD1a or CD207.
Histiocytosis encompasses a range of conditions in which there is abnormal proliferation or differentiation and function of the mononuclear phagocyte system. LCH is the most common histiocyte disorder, with clinical presentations ranging from multisystem disease to single indolent lesions. RDD is also called sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy due to its propensity to cause large lymphadenopathy, and has a wide range of clinical presentations. Mixed type histiocytosis—as in our patient—is an unusual but well documented occurrence. Usually, treatment for histiocytosis is tailored to the individual. However, in severe, multifocal disease and in low-income and middle-income settings where sophisticated histopathological analysis may not be available, it might be appropriate to treat patients with chemotherapy empirically.

input: A 35-year-old man presented to our department with palpitations and mild shortness of breath. He was of Haitian origin and had emigrated to the USA when he was 24 years old. A physical examination, an electrocardiogram (ECG), a full blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic profile showed no abnormalities. However, a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 3 cm × 2 cm echolucent lesion in the apex of the left ventricle (figure; video 1). The patient did not report having a fever or any other systemic problems, but he had been to Haiti 5 months earlier. A cardiac MRI showed a solitary, avascular lesion located in the anterior wall of the left ventricle (figure; video 2); this lesion had no communication with the left ventricular cavity and was non-fatty and cystic. No pericardial or valvular abnormalities were seen. A CT scan of the heart confirmed the lesion was cystic and without any calcification; the coronary arteries were normal and, importantly, were not compressed by the mass. CT scans and MRIs of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no further cysts in any other organs. Serum serology by western blot testing for antibodies against specific IgG glycoproteins was negative for Echinococcus granulosus and Trypanosoma cruzi but positive for Taenia solium. The patient was then treated for 2 weeks with oral albendazole 400 mg twice a day. He reported no further symptoms and the lesion was no longer visible on a further transthoracic echocardiogram (figure; video 3) repeated 1 week after completing the treatment; a repeat cardiac MRI showed that the lesion had decreased considerably in size. Cysticercosis is endemic in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. The disease can develop after consuming foods contaminated with faeces that contain T solium eggs shed from a human carrier. The brain, skeletal muscle, and subcutaneous tissue are involved most frequently; isolated cardiac cysticercosis is rare. The need for concomitant treatment with steroids—particularly in neurocysticercosis—has been much debated because of concerns about seizures and worsening neurological symptoms on the initiation of anthelmintic therapy. In cases of isolated cardiac cysticercosis, there is no consensus for the routine use of steroids. In our patient, given that there was only mild oedema around the solitary lesion, the ECG was normal, and because he was on a cardiac monitor in hospital when albendazole was started, we were able to keep him under observation. Furthermore, it is of note that in other inflammatory cardiac conditions—such as pericarditis—steroids have been linked to increased relapse and recurrence. The rapid response to anthelmintic therapy in this case—reassuringly confirmed on repeat imaging—shows that in select cases, such as this one, albendazole may be used without steroids, with close clinical and cardiac monitoring and serial imaging.

A 40-year-old man attended our ophthalmology department reporting a gradual worsening of vision in both eyes over the previous few months.The patient had a history of sensorineural hearing loss and he had received a kidney transplant at age 19 years; he had previously been diagnosed with X-linked Alport syndrome. Genetic testing, at the time, showed a mutation in the COL4A5 gene. The kidney was donated by the patient's healthy father; the patient has one healthy brother and no children. His mother was identified as the carrier and she was also affected by the disease. The patient was prescribed sirolimus 3 mg daily and prednisolone 5 mg daily.
On general examination, he was well. Regarding his eyes, a slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed a clear crystalline lens with an anterior lenticonus—a subtle protrusion of the anterior surface—in both eyes (figure); the protrusion was clearly visible on anterior segment swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT; figure) and was also detected as an oil-droplet sign with retro-illumination (figure).
Additionally, the patient showed the typical retinal findings of Alport syndrome: central fleck retinopathy—seen as scattered pigmentation irregularities around the macula, which were more obvious on red free images (figure)—temporal retinal thinning on retinal OCT (figure), and peripheral retinopathy. His best corrected vision was reduced to 20/40 (typical 20/20) in both eyes.
We implanted a toric intraocular lens with extended depth of focus in both eyes after lens removal, which improved his vision to 20/25 bilaterally. At 3 months follow-up, the patient had a full corrected distance visual acuity of 20/20.
Alport syndrome is a rare, progressive, hereditary glomerular disease characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, and progressive impairment of kidney function caused by mutations in the COL4A5, usually inherited as X-linked—as in our patient—and COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes, which are transmitted in either an autosomal recessive or dominant pattern. The mutations disrupt collagen type IV synthesis, which is a crucial component of the basal membrane in the renal glomerulus, cochlea, cornea, lens capsule, retina, and skin.
Visual impairment is mostly caused by anterior lenticonus—even if there is no cataract present; it is diagnostic for Alport syndrome, seen in 50% of patients, and can be treated effectively with lens replacement. Central and peripheral retinopathy is seen in 70% and 80% of patients, respectively, and usually does not affect vision. Lenticonus and central retinopathy are predictive for sensorineural hearing loss and renal failure before the age of 30 years. Therefore, in young men with hearing loss and haematuria, an eye examination can give helpful information in confirming the diagnosis of Alport syndrome.
options: Systemic amyloidosis, Alport syndrome, Retinitis pigmentosa, Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis syndrome

input: A 5-year-old boy presented to our department with a 2-day history of acute febrile illness. During evaluation, his blood samples were found to be so lipaemic (figure) that it caused interference in analyte measurements. The child was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, there was no history of failure to thrive or developmental delay, and there were no reports of any previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Neither xanthomata nor hepatosplenomegaly was found at clinical examination. Laboratory test results found a normal fasting blood glucose concentration (4·5 mmol/L). However, triglycerides were found to be very high at 21·4 mmol/L (normal level <1·7 mmol/L). Total serum cholesterol was 5·5 mmol/L (normal level <5·2 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol by direct measurement was 0·7 mmol/L (normal level <2·6 mmol/L), and HDL cholesterol was 0·5 mmol/L (normal level >1·0 mmol/L). Investigations for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia were negative. Dilated fundus examination showed creamy white discolouration of retinal blood vessels (figure) suggestive of lipaemia retinalis; no retinal haemorrhages or exudates were seen. Fasting lipid profiles of other family members were normal. Taking into account the young age of the patient, the lipaemic plasma, the hypertriglyceridaemia, the lipaemia retinalis, and the lack of indications that his difficulties were secondary to any other diseases causing hypertriglyceridaemia, the boy was diagnosed with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS). As treatment is mainly dietary fat restriction, the child was started on a low-fat diet—less than 10% of total calories—with medium-chain triglyceride supplements.FCS is characterised by impaired or absent activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)—the key enzyme in catabolism of triglyceride rich lipoproteins, particularly chylomicrons. LPL is also involved in the accumulation of chylomicrons which give the milky appearance of the plasma. Bi-allelic mutations in the LPL gene account for around 80% of cases of FCS; the remainder are caused by mutations in one of four genes encoding proteins that interact with LPL. Early recognition and treatment of hyperlipidaemia are crucial to prevent systemic complications like acute pancreatitis. Many patients with elevated triglycerides do not have lipaemia retinalis for reasons that are unclear. The lipaemic appearance of the retinal blood vessels may persist after normalisation of the triglycerides on laboratory testing. Most systemic diseases have eye signs. The importance of an ophthalmological examination as a crucial component of a thorough medical examination cannot be overlooked.
options: LDL receptor, Lipoprotein lipase, Hormone-sensitive lipase, Proprotein convertase subtilisin / kexin type 9

input: A 34-year old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and portal hypertension, presented with abdominal distension and pain of 2 weeks' duration. Examination showed Cullen's sign (periumbilical ecchymosis; figure A), Grey-Turner's sign (ecchymosis on the abdominal flank; figure B) and ascites. A working diagnosis of acute pancreatitis seemed reasonable because both Cullen's and Grey-Turner's signs are associated with severe necrotising pancreatitis. Laboratory tests showed anaemia, normal leucocyte and platelet counts, and a mildly deranged coagulation profile, with an international normalised ratio of 1·6. Serum amylase, lipase, and α-fetoprotein were within normal limits. A four-quadrant abdominal tap showed uniformly bloody fluid. Analysis of the fluid showed a leucocyte count of 0·15×109 per L (60% neutrophils), which was not consistent with an infectious cause, a high serum ascitic albumin gradient of 1·4, and normal adenine deaminase values. Malignant cells were not seen and no organisms were detected on gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen stain, or cultures. PCR for acid-fast bacilli was negative. Chest radiography was unremarkable. Tuberculin test (1TU) was negative. Ultrasonography and MRI of the abdomen showed hepatomegaly, ascites, and evidence of portal hypertension; the pancreas was normal on imaging studies. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed grade II oesophageal varices. A diagnosis of haemoperitoneum possibly due to rupture of intra-abdominal varices secondary to portal hypertension was made. Cullen's and Grey-Turner's signs have been described with intra-abdominal haemorrhage most commonly associated with pancreatitis. Rare associations include ectopic pregnancy, malignant disease (liver, abdominal metastasis), perforated duodenal ulcer, liver abscess, and splenic rupture.

A previously well 79-year-old woman presented with the acute onset of coffee-ground emesis. She had no previous history of alcohol intake, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or ingestion of corrosive agents. Urgent oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was done. She was kept nil-orally and commenced on an intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, fluconazole, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a diffuse black appearance of the mucosa from the mid-oesophagus to the gastro-oesophageal junction (figure A), where there was a clearly demarcated boundary with normal mucosa (figure B)—a finding consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis. This condition is also known as Gurvits' syndrome or black oesophagus. Acute oesophageal necrosis is a rare clinical entity that usually presents with either frank haematemesis or coffee-ground emesis. It has a characteristic endoscopic appearance of circumferential, friable, black-coloured mucosa in the distal oesophagus that ends clearly and abruptly at the gastro-oesophageal junction. It is thought to be caused by oesophageal ischaemia. Multiple factors might be involved, including haemodynamic compromise, malnutrition, drug ingestion, and underlying cardiovascular or renal disease. Although the oesophagus is largely protected from ischaemia by its complex and intricate anastomotic vascular network, there is a watershed area in the distal oesophagus that is more susceptible to ischaemic injury. Management of acute oesophageal necrosis generally involves resuscitation, supportive measures, and treatment of any coexisting illness. Antimicrobial therapy is usually unnecessary, except in the setting of oesophageal perforation, positive cultures, or suspected sepsis. Although complications of perforation and stricture formation are uncommon, acute oesophageal necrosis carries a high overall mortality risk due to its association with other comorbidities and critical illness. However, acute oesophageal necrosis in an otherwise healthy patient often resolves spontaneously and is associated with a more favourable outcome.Repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopy of our patient 72 h later revealed complete resolution of the initial endoscopic findings (figure C). Our patient was subsequently discharged home following resolution of the injury and remains well at 6-month follow-up.
options: Oesophageal acanthosis nigricans, Acute oesophageal necrosis, Malignant melanoma of the oesophagus, Oesophageal melanocytosis

A 26-year-old woman with a 2-year history of swelling of her eyelids and reduced vision was referred to our clinic by an ophthalmologist because of increased myopia, decreased visual acuity, scattered pale dots of the maculae, and suspected angioedema.
The patient had been diagnosed with attention deficit disorder and had been prescribed methylphenidate since adolescence. 5 years before we saw her, she reported having occasional episodes of dizziness thought to be caused by anaemia—investigations at that stage had found an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR; 134 mm/h; typical rate 0–20) and a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 9·5 g/dL; typical range 11·7–15·5). The patient had been found to have hepatitis C genotype 3 but was temporarily lost to follow-up.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well but lethargic; she was thin with a BMI of 13·9 kg/m2 (typical range 18·5–25·0). She had bilateral upper and lower palpebral oedema (figure 1) and diminished visual acuity. Oedema was noted also in the face and lips; but despite slight distal lower extremity hyperalgesia and uncertainty of balance and side steps in tandem walk, there were no other abnormalities found.Fundoscopic examination showed abundant pale dots around the maculae and peripherally in the retinae (figure 2) indicating a crystal retinopathy; optical coherence tomography confirmed the diagnosis showing numerous retinal white dots, oedema of both fovea, and submacular cysts (figure 2).Laboratory investigations found that both the anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8·2 g/dL) and the elevated ESR (129 mm/h) persisted. A comprehensive metabolic panel—which included tests for plasma C-reactive protein concentration, sodium concentration, potassium concentration, creatinine concentration, calcium concentration, glucose concentration, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, thromboplastin time, amylase, cortisol, free thyroxine, thyroid stimulating hormone, angiotensin converting enzyme, and immunoglobulin subclass analysis—and urinalysis found no abnormalities. Tests for infectious mononucleosis and HIV were negative; plasma albumin was 31 g/L (normal range 36–48) and prealbumin 0·13 g/L (normal range 0·23–0·37).
18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the whole body showed no signs of systemic disease, infection, or cancer. An electrocardiogram showed inverted T waves in the anterior leads; an echocardiogram showed mild enlargement of the right heart with a small pericardial effusion. Systolic flattening of the interventricular septum was present. Trace tricuspid regurgitation was seen. Right heart catheterisation confirmed precapillary pulmonary hypertension.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a bone marrow biopsy showed abundant foamy macrophage infiltration characterised by clear cytoplasm (figure 2); additionally, histiocytes in the bone marrow contained dark pigmented fragments—consistent with titanium deposits that can be associated with intravenous substance use. Furthermore, serum chitotriosidase activity was elevated (1036 nmol/h per mL; typical range 0–195), indicating possible increased macrophage activity or any of several lysosomal storage disorders. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed the patient had impairments of both short-term memory and executive functioning.
Brain MRI with contrast showed diffuse dural thickening and enhancement without any focal pathology of the brain (figure 2). Histopathologic examination of a sample obtained from dural biopsy indicated clusters of CD68-positive macrophages (figure 2); analyses of samples of biopsies from the skin and of biopsies obtained during a gastroscopy were normal.
At this stage our working diagnoses included chronic hepatitis C, severe protein energy malnutrition, secondary pulmonary hypertension, talc retinopathy, secondary histiocytosis, pachymeningitis, amyloidosis, and IgG4 disease.
Whole exome sequencing ruled out inherited causes of primary or secondary histiocytosis. On closer questioning, the patient said she had been intravenously injecting methylphenidate hydrochloride by dissolving the core of the tablets in water. Methylphenidate tablets contain titanium and high molecular weight polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as an adjuvant—a substance associated with histiocytosis when used parenterally. A diagnosis of PVP histiocytosis was made. The patient was counselled and informed of the diagnosis and advised to avoid intravenous substance use. At follow-up 1 year later, she was more alert than before, and her appetite had improved; ESR had decreased ranging from 26 mm/h to 38 mm/h suggesting discontinuation of active intravenous substance use.
Bilateral swelling of the eyelids or periorbital oedema can be caused by nephrotic syndrome, thyroid eye disease, systemic infections such as mononucleosis, atopic or allergic swelling, sarcoidosis, dermatomyositis, lymphoma, IgG4 disease, and various histiocytoses. PVP is widely used in prescription drugs. Moderate and high molecular weight PVP is only used in oral preparations; when used intravenously patients may have renal insufficiency, anaemia, pathological fractures, and abdominal complaints. PVP can be deposited in most organs leading to severe dysfunction. Earlier intravenous abuse of oral PVP containing buprenorphine and methadone preparations, for maintenance therapy for opioid dependence, has been reported to cause severe, and even lethal PVP histiocytosis.

input:
A woman aged 28 years with systemic lupus erythematous and abnormal kidney function, treated with 4·5 mg/kg hydroxychloroquine daily for 15 years (cumulative dose 1369 g), presented with bilateral progressive central vision loss for 2 months. The patient had no known previous exposure to chloroquine. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/40 in her right eye and 20/30 in her left eye. Funduscopy showed a concentric hypopigmentation around both foveas (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography of the macula revealed photoreceptor layer and retinal pigmented epithelium loss, and automated 24-2 visual fields showed bilateral central scotomas (figure). These findings were consistent with bull's eye maculopathy, a classic feature of advanced hydroxychloroquine toxicity. 3 months after medication was stopped, the patient's visual acuity had remained stable, and no other complaints were reported.Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial drug commonly used in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematous, rheumatoid arthritis, and other connective tissue disorders. Its toxic effect on the retina is due to its ability to bind melanin in the retinal pigmented epithelium. Early toxicity might be asymptomatic or the patient might complain of colour vision changes and paracentral scotomas. When the classic fundus findings are present, as in our patient, the scotomas might not resolve and the retinal damage might progress despite discontinuation of the drug. The dose (>5·0 mg/kg) and duration of treatment (>5 years), and concomitant renal disease and tamoxifen use are important risk factors for the development of maculopathy.
In 2016, the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommended a baseline fundus examination to be done during the first year of starting the drug and annual screening after 5 years of treatment, using automated visual fields plus spectral domain optical coherence tomography for patients on acceptable doses (ie, <5·0 mg/kg) and without major risk factors. Hence, it is hoped that with proper dosage and regular screening, bull's eye maculopathy will rarely occur.
options: Corticosteroids, Hydroxychloroquine, Methotrexate, Azathioprine

input: A 43-year-old man presented with cough and expectoration for 7 days. Since birth he had had recurrent episodes of respiratory tract infections, for which he used to take drugs from his family doctor. He was married for 15 years but had borne no children. On examination, apex beat was in the sixth right intercostal space with heart sounds being heard on the right side of the chest. Electrocardiogram showed evidence of dextrocardia (figure A). Cardiac apex, along with aortic arch and gastric bubble on chest radiograph were seen on the right side (figure B). High-resolution CT of chest and upper abdomen showed bronchiectasis (figure C) with situs inversus totalis (figure D). Radiograph and CT of sinuses showed mucosal thickening in maxillary sinuses and hypoplastic frontal sinuses. Fibreoptic bronchoscopy showed transposition of right and left bronchus. Semen analysis (done thrice) showed decreased sperm viability with no motility. Saccharin test for mucociliary clearance gave a time of 48 min (normal <15 min). A diagnosis of Kartagener's syndrome was made. Kartagener's syndrome is characterised by the triad of chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus. It is classified under the group of disorders called primary ciliary dyskinesias. Patients generally present with recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract infection because of ineffective mucociliary clearance. As sperm mortility is dependent on ciliary function, males are generally sterile.
options: An atrial septal defect, Situs inversus, Kartagener's syndrome, Young's syndrome

A 60-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve and dilatation of the ascending aorta had surgical bioprosthesis implantation with aortic repair. 6 weeks after the sternotomy scar had completely healed, several soft nodules appeared progressively along the scar without pus or grains (figure, A). He had no fever, pain, or erythema on the sternal area. Laboratory tests showed normal leucocytosis, and C-reactive protein was 190·48 nmol/L. Cultures of cutaneous swabs and biopsy samples grew meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Mycobacterial and fungal cultures were negative. Investigation of skin biopsy samples showed a dermal polymorphic infiltrate with epithelioid and giant cell granulomas without necrosis or grains (figure, B). Periodic-acid Schiff, Gram, Grocott, and Zielh stains were negative. Thoracic CT revealed a sternum osteolysis with periosteal reaction and bone disjunction (figure, C). Sternum osteitis was confirmed by surgical findings and cultures of bone sample, positive for MSSA. The treatment combined surgical drainage and antibiotic therapy with 1 week of intravenous cefamandole followed by oral ofloxacine and rifampicin for 3 months. The patient did not relapse during more than 15 months of follow-up.Botryomycosis is a rare, chronic, and granulomatous cutaneous bacterial infection mostly due to Staphylococcus aureus, presenting as nodules typically characterised by the formation of grains. However, lesions can be atypical, similar to pyogenic granulomas. Cutaneous lesions usually reveal underlying, chronic soft tissue, muscle, or bone staphylococcal infection, as in our case. Pathophysiology of botryomycosis involves a balance between a low virulence of the bacteria and host resistance.
When presented with such lesions, clinicians should look for an underlying bone or soft tissue staphylococcal infection, especially in patients who have had recent surgery.

input: A 51-year-old man who had been receiving haemodialysis for 15 years was referred to the Toranomon Hospital (Tokyo, Japan) with progressive calcified nodules on his fingers. He had been undergoing haemodialysis three times per week, for a total of 12 h per week. The patient had been deemed to have end-stage renal disease of unknown cause. He had undergone a parathyroidectomy 2 years before the referral because he was believed to have progressive extraskeletal calcification caused by hyperparathyroidism with constant hypercalcaemia that was refractory to medical treatment; laboratory findings were compatible with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Since the parathyroidectomy, laboratory findings had returned to normal, but the nodules had progressed and made him unable to grip. A family history could not be obtained because the patient was an orphan, but through a careful interview we identified a past medical history of recurrent urolithiasis, which was judged to be the leading cause of the end-stage renal disease. Physical examination showed clubbed fingers with exposed calcified masses (figure A). Radiography showed prominent bilateral calcified deposits (figure B) and nephrocalcinosis. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry-based plasma metabolomic assessment showed substantially increased concentrations of oxalate (316 μmol/L) and glycerate (50·2 μmol/L; normal is <10 μmol/L for both), but glycolate concentration was almost normal at 13·3 μmol/L (normal is <12 μmol/L), suggesting the possibility of primary hyperoxaluria type 2. Genetic analysis showed a missense mutation, 181G→A (Asp61Asn), of GRHPR in exon 2. We therefore diagnosed the patient as having primary hyperoxaluria type 2 and started intensive haemodialysis (25 h per week, Monday to Friday, for 2 years so far) in preparation for renal transplantation. The patient is currently on a waiting list for renal transplantation.Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by mutation of GRHPR, the gene encoding the enzyme glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase, which results in hyperoxaluria, recurrent urolithiasis, progressive nephrocalcinosis, end-stage renal disease, and, eventually, systemic oxalate deposition. Primary hyperoxaluria type 2, especially when associated with renal failure and caused by plasma oxalate concentrations exceeding the supersaturation index of oxalate in plasma (30 μmol/L), should be identified early because severe manifestations, as seen in our patient, can be prevented with early diagnosis, intensive management of dialysis, and timely transplantation.

A 32-year-old woman, who was 12 weeks pregnant, was referred to our emergency department feeling generally unwell after recurrent vomiting. She had no notable medical history.On arrival at the hospital, she was mildly confused and reported polyuria. On clinical examination she was unwell and showed signs of dehydration; her pulse was 119 beats per min and her blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, and temperature 37°C. An electrocardiogram showed a prolonged PR interval and repolarisation was abnormal.
Laboratory investigations found a serum potassium concentration of 3 mmol/L (normal range 3·5–5·1) and a serum creatine concentration of 43 μmol/L (normal range 64–104); the patient's thyroid hormone concentrations were normal. Total serum calcium and phosphorus concentrations were 4·15 mmol/L (normal range 2·20–2·55) and 1·02 mmol/L (normal range 0·8–1·5), respectively; serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration was 992 pg/mL (normal range 6–50).
We made a working diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism presenting as a hypercalcaemic crisis. The patient was rehydrated with a saline infusion of 5 L given over 24 h and an intravenous infusion of calcitonin—100 U over 8 h—under cardiac monitoring. After 48 h, as the patient's serum calcium had reduced to 3·89 mmol/L, but still above normal range, cinacalcet was added at a dose of 30 mg every 8 h. The clinical condition of the patient improved, but after 72 h, severe hypercalcaemia (3·40 mmol/L) persisted. Two sessions of dialysis using a low-calcium dialysate transiently lowered the serum calcium level; the patient's albumin-adjusted serum calcium concentration remained stable at 3·1 mmol/L, while she was given a saline infusion, calcitonin, and cinacalcet.
A cervical ultrasound showed a 27 mm × 12 mm × 8 mm, highly hypoechoic oval thyroid nodule vascularised in the periphery of the right thyroid lobe—suggestive of a malignant lesion—which we graded 5 on the European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (figure). No lesions in the usual parathyroid sites were seen. A cervicothoracic CT scan confirmed the intrathyroid lesion and showed no evidence of parathyroid adenoma in the usual or ectopic sites (figure). We did a fine needle aspiration and PTH concentration—measured in the evacuated aspirate—was found to be very high (1495 pg/mL), indicative of a parathyroid adenoma. Notably, PTH is normally undetectable in non-parathyroid tissue. Additionally, parathyroid scintigraphy, which would have helped localise the lesion, is currently unavailable in French Guiana. The patient had an emergency operation to remove the intrathyroid lesion (figure). Serum PTH and calcium concentrations reduced from preoperative levels of 1465 pg/mL and 3·22 mmol/L, respectively to 103 pg/mL and 3·06 mmol/L intraoperatively, and to 16 pg/mL and 2·7 mmol/L immediately postoperatively. Histopathological examination of a sample of the excised lesion confirmed a parathyroid adenoma (figure). Postoperatively, the patient's general condition markedly improved; a fetal ultrasound showed no abnormalities, and the remainder of the patient's pregnancy was uneventful.
Diagnosing hypercalcaemia during pregnancy can be difficult. Symptoms—including nausea, vomiting, and fatigue—are like those of early pregnancy. Furthermore, long-standing hypercalcaemia may lead to preeclampsia, which in early pregnancy can lead to shortness of breath, tachycardia, and confusion; both mother and child's needs must be considered during management and treatment. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause, and adenomas may be difficult to find. Fine needle aspiration and PTH measurement in the aspirate may be an alternative method of diagnosis—particularly in resource-limited settings.
options: Preeclampsia and hypertension, Pancreatitis and nephrolithiasis, Diplopia and nystagmus, Depression and anxiety

A 24-year-old woman attended our follow-up clinic reporting that the multiple tendinous and cutaneous xanthomas on her hands, elbows, and feet had markedly improved (figure).The patient had developed the lesions on her hands and feet, aged 2 years. Laboratory investigations, done at the time, showed marked hyperlipidaemia with a total cholesterol concentration of 21·3 mmol/L (typical level 5 or below) and a low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol concentration of 18·5 mmol/L (typical range 1·81–3·62). She had been diagnosed with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH). Genetic testing, done at the time of diagnosis, found biallelic mutations of the LDL receptor (LDLR) gene (c.681C>G and c.1285G>A). Additionally, the patient's mother was heterozygous for the FH Afrikaner-2 mutation (c.1285G>A) but had no evidence of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; her father was heterozygous for the FH Afrikaner-1 mutation (c.681C>G) and had a coronary stent inserted when he was aged 46 years. The patient's brother had been diagnosed with HoFH and had died from atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease aged 6 years.
From the time of diagnosis, different lipid-lowering therapies were added to the patient's treatment as newer agents became available. A high-intensity statin (atorvastatin) was prescribed when she was 2 years old; ezetimibe, which inhibits cholesterol absorption from the intestine, was included when she was 8 years; and evolocumab, a proprotein convertase subtilisin-kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitor, was given at age 15 years. However, despite the triple therapy, the patient's LDL cholesterol concentration remained elevated at 16·3 mmol/L. Notably, lipoprotein apheresis—indicated at this stage—was not available at our centre.
At 16 years of age, the patient had an aortic valve replacement because of severe atherosclerotic valvular stenosis.
At 22 years of age, she was commenced on the intravenous angiopoietin-like protein 3 (ANGPTL3) monoclonal antibody, evinacumab, at a dose of 15 mg/kg each month and within 2 months her LDL cholesterol concentration was reduced by 77% to 3·73 mmol/L. Continued treatment over the next 2 years resulted in gradual—yet marked—regression for her cutaneous xanthomata (figure).
HoFH results in very high levels of LDL cholesterol from birth and carries an extremely high risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. HoFH continues to be underdiagnosed. In low-income countries diagnosis is mainly based on clinical findings—the presence of interdigital cutaneous xanthomata, for example, as seen in our patient, is regarded as pathognomonic. Two pathogenic allelic variants at the LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, or LDLRAP1 gene loci cause the disease.
LDL receptor-independent therapies—such as ANGPTL3 inhibitors and lipoprotein apheresis—are crucial means of lowering LDL-C in individuals with HoFH. Significant lowering of LDL-C can lead to regression of xanthomata, but more importantly reduces the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (video).
options: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins), PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab), Bempedoic acid, ANGPTL3 inhibitors (evinacumab)

A 60-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with a 4-day history of mild, diffuse abdominal pain and discomfort in her abdomen. The patient's medical history was unremarkable apart from a cholelithiasis-related cholecystectomy which had been done 12 years earlier.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; her pulse was 75 beats per min and blood pressure 145/80 mm Hg. She was febrile with a temperature of 38·0°C; she had diffuse left-sided abdominal tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 16 mg/dL (normal <6) and a raised white blood cell (WBC) count of 12·6 × 109 per L (normal range 4–11); carcinoembryonic antigen concentration was within normal range (1·2 ng/mL; typical value for non-smoker or ex-smoker <3·8 and for smokers <5·5).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a 3·3 cm × 2·8 cm × 8·0 cm intramural peripherally enhancing hypodense lesion together with pericolic fat stranding and haziness which had caused mild upstream large bowel distention—we presumed it was an abscess in the large bowel wall; features—colonic wall outpouchings—consistent with a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis were also seen (figure). Importantly, no extraluminal air was seen. Considering the patient's clinical condition, particularly the absence of signs of peritonitis, we decided to manage her conservatively; she was started on intravenous fluids and treated empirically with piperacillin and tazobactam. Over the next few days, the patient's symptoms improved; her temperature, WBC count, and CRP concentration reduced. A repeat CT scan 7 days after admission showed almost complete resolution of original findings—indicating spontaneous resolution of the abscess and further confirming the initial diagnosis (figure). The patient was allowed home 8 days after admission and prescribed oral antimicrobial treatment (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole).
6 weeks later, an outpatient colonoscopy showed mild residual stenosis at the site of the previous intramural abscess with no other abnormalities; the patient reported no symptoms or difficulty passing faeces.
Abscesses complicate 15–30% of acute diverticulitis cases; intramural lesions are infrequently reported. Secondary partial intestinal obstruction may occur, but severe obstruction is rare. In most cases, abscesses spontaneously resolve. Conservative treatment is favoured in smaller-sized abscesses (<3–4 cm); further intervention may be needed for larger ones.
The treatment approach depends upon abscess location and the overall medical condition of the patient; conservative management is preferable. The differential diagnosis of such a lesion should include various types of colitis-related abscesses, inflammatory bowel disease, contained perforations, infected enteric duplication cysts, and, most significantly, colon cancer. Importantly, in patients with radiologically confirmed acute diverticulitis, colonic cancer has been found to have a 1-year incidence rate ranging from 1·6% to 2·7%. To exclude an underlying colonic malignancy, patients with acute diverticulitis are advised to undergo colonoscopy approximately 6–8 weeks following their episode.
options: Inflammatory bowel disease, Large bowel duplication cyst, Intramural large bowel diverticular abscess, Colonic cancer

A 57-year-old woman with a 12-h history of fever and severe pain in her back, pelvis, and thighs attended our hospital. 24 h earlier, the patient had the first dose of inotuzumab ozogamicin at 0·8 mg/m2 intravenously for primary refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. 2 months earlier, she had presented with pneumonia and was found to have anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and circulating B-lymphoblasts in her peripheral blood. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed a diagnosis of Philadelphia chromosome-negative B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with low hypodiploidy; she had been treated according to a modified Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia Consortium Protocol—excluding pegaspargase. She had been given the inotuzumab ozogamicin because post-induction bone marrow showed refractory disease (appendix).
The patient had a history of hypothyroidism and was prescribed levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, citalopram 20 mg daily, and valacyclovir 500 mg daily.
On examination, she was in distress because of the diffuse bone pain; but her vital signs and physical examination were otherwise normal, and she was afebrile.
Laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 2·37 × 109 per L (typical range 4·5–11·0), haemoglobin concentration was 93 g/L (typical range 120–160), and platelet count was 117 × 109 per L (typical range 150–400); a blood film was leukoerythroblastic. C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was 59 mg/L (typical concentration <5), D-dimer concentration was 29 196 ng/mL (typical concentration <500), ferritin concentration was 20 498 μg/L (typical range 6·5–204), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) concentration was 5 435 U/L (typical concentration <230). Other liver enzyme concentrations were mildly elevated, fibrinogen was normal, as was CT scan of the lumbar spine. Over the next 2 days, her CRP rose to 359 mg/L, ferritin to 105 204 μg/L, and LDH to >7325 U/L. Blood cultures and viral load tests for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr were negative.
The bone marrow aspirate was a dry tap, but histopathological examination of a sample obtained from a trephine biopsy showed extensive necrosis with no haematopoietic tissue present (figure); notably, the post-induction bone marrow—examined 18 days earlier—was hypercellular at 90% (normocellular marrow is defined as 30–70) with 80% B-lymphoblasts.
Treatment with dexamethasone and tocilizumab was commenced, followed by anakinra—specifically to treat the hyperinflammatory syndrome—which resulted in improvement in the patient's pain and normalisation of the acute phase reactants. Subsequent acute lymphoblastic leukaemia-directed therapy included a cycle of dose-adjusted hyperfractionated cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone. 23 days following chemotherapy, the white blood cell and platelet counts normalised with a persistent moderate anaemia seen; a bone marrow biopsy still showed signs of necrosis but no evidence of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
Inotuzumab ozogamicin, an anti-CD22 antibody conjugated with the toxin calicheamicin, has been shown to be effective in relapsed B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; recognised adverse effects include myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity. Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like manifestations—a recognised variant of cytokine release syndrome and a feature of hyperinflammation—have been seen with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy targeting CD22 in patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Additionally, bone marrow necrosis has been described following treatment with blinatumomab and mitoxantrone, etoposide, and intermediate dose cytarabine. Neither hyperinflammation nor bone marrow necrosis has, as far as we are aware, been reported with inotuzumab ozogamicin.
Hyperinflammation presents with fever and elevated serum acute phase reactants such as C-reactive protein, ferritin, and D-dimer. With bone marrow necrosis, patients generally have a fever and back pain, as well as cytopenia, leukoerythroblastic blood film, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase. Prompt treatment typically involves removing the trigger—in our case the inotuzumab ozogamicin—and addressing the underlying cause; anti-inflammatory therapies, such as corticosteroids and cytokine inhibition, are sometimes employed. Early consideration of rare but serious immune-mediated adverse effects of antibody-drug conjugate therapy can guide timely and appropriate management.

input: A 94-year-old woman was referred to a dermatology clinic with a painless, smooth, hard swelling over the proximal interphalangeal joint of her left little finger (figure). The swelling had been present for 20 years. We could see yellow-white material under the skin. The patient had similar changes over the metatarsal joints of her feet, with overlying ulceration. Skin biopsy and aspiration of joint fluid excluded calciphylaxis, and confirmed that the patient had urate deposits (tophi)—ie, gout. Microscopy with polarised light showed negatively birefringent urate crystals. The serum concentration of urate was 530 μmol/L (normal concentration 60–360 μmol/L). We prescribed allopurinol. A 13-year-old boy was admitted to hospital with a low-grade fever (maximum temperature of 38°C) that had persisted for 6 months. During this time, his body temperature typically increased in the afternoon or evening and was accompanied by arthralgia, mild headache, and cough. The patient did not report any other clinical signs or symptoms. His white blood cell count, haemoglobin concentration, platelet count, C-reactive protein concentration, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were all normal. No bacterial or fungal infections were detected in the blood, bone marrow, or cerebrospinal fluid cultures. Ultrasound examination revealed multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the neck, bilateral subclavian region, abdominal cavity, and groin. The patient had previously been treated with piperacillin-tazobactam and aciclovir, but showed no improvement. His past medical history and family history were unremarkable.An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET-CT scan revealed a symmetrical increase in FDG metabolism in multiple cartilages (figure A, B). The maximum standard uptake value of the lesions was 5·4, and whole-exome sequencing revealed a pathogenic variant of the NLRP12 gene (1742G→A, Trp581*; accession number VCV001444965.2, variation ID 1444965), which has been reported in several cases associated with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. The pathogenicity of this mutation was assessed using InterVar, a bioinformatics software tool, which predicted very strong (PVS1), moderate (PM2), and supporting (PP3) evidence of pathogenicity. However, this mutation was classified as a variant of uncertain significance in the ClinVar database, so interpretation of the pathogenicity of this mutation should still be approached with caution. The patient was treated with 20 mg of methylprednisolone per day for 5 days and was then discharged with no fever or arthralgia. After 4 months, the 18F-FDG PET-CT scan was repeated and indicated that the polychondritis was in complete remission (figure C, D).
To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of polychondritis occurring in a patient with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. This result could partly explain why the patient did not have elevated inflammatory indicators, which is observed in 30% of people with autoinflammatory diseases associated with NLRP12 mutations. The clinical features of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease differ from familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, as only about 47% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease have clear triggers from exposure to cold. Furthermore, the median age of onset for NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease is higher than NLRP3-related autoinflammatory disease, and headaches are an uncommon finding observed in approximately 14% of patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease. Regarding this patient, we suspect that his arthralgia could indicate chondritic pain.
Most patients with NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease benefit from a short regimen of corticosteroid treatment without requiring additional interleukin-1 blocking therapy. Both NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and polychondritis are rare diseases that are associated with immune system disorders. Due to the rarity of NLRP12-related autoinflammatory disease and the diverse range of associated clinical manifestations, many clinicians have an insufficient understanding of this condition. Auxiliary diagnostic techniques, such as 18F-FDG PET-CT, can help to expand the spectrum of clinical features associated with the disease and monitor the effectiveness of treatment in conjunction with other relevant clinical data. The complete remission seen in this patient with methylprednisolone treatment supports the effectiveness of this therapy for polychondritis associated with NLRP12 mutations.
options: VEXAS syndrome, MAGIC syndrome, NLRP12-autoinflammatory disease, Chronic infantile neurological, cutaneous, articular syndrome

A 13-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of mild pain in her right knee. She reported no recent injury. x-rays showed a high-density linear abnormality with a periosteal reaction in the proximal right tibia (figure), which medical staff, at the hospital where she was first seen, thought might have been a tumour of the bone.On examination in our hospital, we found the patient to have some tenderness in the proximal right tibia with no swelling, ecchymosis, or any obvious deformity. The patient had normal range of movement of the knee and no restriction in squatting.
MRI showed a rough hypointense fracture line surrounded by an extensive hyperintense area of bone marrow oedema in the T2-weighted image (figure) clearly indicating a fracture of the tibia. Further, on closer questioning, the patient remembered that she had recently fallen on her knees while walking. After 4 weeks of rest and restricted weight bearing, the patient had no further trouble with pain during daily activity.
An x-ray repeated 4 weeks after the initial presentation showed a healed fracture with obvious bone callus formation (figure); the repeat MRI showed that the bone marrow oedema had receded (figure).
An occult fracture—often known as a bone contusion or bone bruising—is defined as a fracture that cannot be seen on conventional x-ray or radiographically shows subtle abnormalities which are prone to be overlooked or misdiagnosed at initial presentation. The history of a single traumatic event is an important clue in diagnosing an occult fracture and if suspected, MRI or CT can help confirm the diagnosis and assist in the evaluation of the lesion. In most cases the bone marrow oedema will completely disappear after 6–12 weeks. For most occult fractures without severe ligament or articular cartilage injury, conservative therapy is the first-line treatment—including analgesia treatment and weight-bearing restriction.
In children with symptoms of swelling, pain, or redness, and a fracture of the bone—particularly either side of the knee or in the upper arm—the diagnosis must be considered to be a malignancy until proven otherwise.
options: Ewing’s sarcoma, Occult fracture, Osteosarcoma, Osteomyelitis

A 15-year-old male patient presented with constipation, abdominal pain, occasional non-bilious vomit, and passage of foul-smelling stool mixed with multiple gravel stones. The patient did not have oliguria, fever, rectal bleeding, or any features suggestive of peritonitis, and was not on any regular medication. He had a similar history of passage of stones 3 months previously, which had resolved spontaneously. The patient had a history of pica but no other psychiatric disorder or developmental delay.On examination, we found diffuse abdominal tenderness with normal bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination revealed a so-called colonic crunch sign. The patient's complete haemogram and blood biochemistry, including serum calcium, phosphorus, and parathyroid hormone, were within normal limits. Straight abdominal radiography revealed multiple opaque shadows of different sizes scattered throughout the colon, with a corn-on-the-cob-like appearance (figure A), consistent with a diagnosis of lithobezoars. The patient was treated conservatively with laxatives and after 5 days, repeat abdominal radiography showed a near complete resolution (figure B). The patient passed multiple stones (figure C), chemical analysis of which showed they were composed of aluminium silicate.
Pica is considered normal in children younger than 2 years of age, but is rare above the age of 5 years. The aetiology of pica is unknown, but is postulated to be multifactorial, including iron-deficiency anaemia and different psychiatric disorders. A bezoar is a mass found trapped in the gastrointestinal tract. Bezoars can be composed of different materials such as hair (tricobezoars), vegetable material (phytobezoars), milk (lactobezoars), sand, and, rarely, stones (lithobezoars). Other causes of colonic calcifications include phlebosclerotic colitis, lanthanum, and parasitic infections such as schistosomiasis. Absence of specific predisposing factors such as old age, history of haematochaezia, chronic renal failure, atherosclerotic vascular disease (for phlebosclerotic colitis), specific drug intake (lanthanum as a phosphate binder), and the presence of a colonic crunch sign and a typical radiological corn-on-the-cob-like appearance helped in the differential diagnosis of our patient.
options: Lanthanum, Lithobezoars, Phlebosclerotic colitis, Schistosomiasis

A full-term infant, weighing 2820 g, born to a 33-year-old healthy primigravida, was referred to us after delivery by emergency caesarean section, because of decreased foetal movements. The baby was also reported to have reduced activity after birth.On examination, we found the patient to be pale. He had delayed capillary refill. Hydrops, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly were absent.
Laboratory investigations showed anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 5·5 g/dL (reference range 12·5–19·5), a raised mean corpuscular volume of 125·9 fL (reference range 91·3–120·0), and an increased reticulocyte count of 22·8% (reference range 2·0–5·4).
Congenital infection screening tests and neonatal screening tests showed no positive findings (appendix). The infant's mother did not have a history of haemoglobinopathies and had the same blood type as her baby: type O positive. The Coombs test was negative. Abdominal and brain sonography showed no haemorrhages.
Polychromasia was found in a peripheral blood smear. The Kleihauer-Betke test showed approximately 10% (reference range 0·0–0·5) of fetal red blood cells (RBCs) in the mother's blood (figure); substantially higher than the typical value.
Considering this information, we diagnosed fetal-maternal haemorrhage (FMH). We subsequently transfused the infant packed RBCs and he was allowed home, fit and well, 21 days after birth.
FMH is characterised by the passage of fetal blood into the mother's circulation either before or at birth. Although fetal problems, placental abnormalities, direct trauma to the abdomen, previous FMH, obstetrical intervention, obstetrical complications, and substance misuse are recognised risk factors for FMH. The cause, in most cases, is unknown. Additionally, depending on the amount of fetal blood loss, and whether it is acute or chronic, the clinical manifestations of FMH can be categorised as asymptomatic or symptomatic with decreased or absent fetal movement, stillbirth, non-immune hydrops fetalis, neonatal anaemia, sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern, and tachyarrhythmia.
The Kleihauer-Betke acid elution test is one of the diagnostic tools of FMH, which results in fetal RBCs remaining pink and adult RBCs becoming colourless—known as ghost cells. The difference in colour is explained by haemoglobin F being stable—compared to haemoglobin A which is unstable—at a low pH. Management options include intrauterine transfusion, emergency delivery by caesarean section, and neonatal transfusion.
options: Rosette screen, Kleihauer-Betke test, Apt-Downey test, Flow cytometry
