A 61-year-old Japanese man with a history of cord-blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia 15 years previously, and chronic graft-versus-host disease of the skin, was admitted for bleeding due to a duodenal ulcer. A maintenance dose of 5 mg prednisone was administered daily. The patient was successfully treated with a combination of endoscopic clipping and proton-pump inhibitor. 7 days after the episode of gastrointestinal bleeding, the patient underwent repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopies, which showed multiple, newly developed, shallow ulcers in the oesophagus. Some of the lesions were circumscribed and discrete (figure).An oesophageal biopsy of the lesions was done, and histopathology of the oesophagus showed ballooning degeneration and multinucleated epithelial giant cells with eosinophilic intracellular inclusion bodies (figure). The biopsy samples showed neither malignancy nor graft-versus-host disease. Immunohistochemical staining of the specimens was also positive for herpes simplex virus, but negative for cytomegalovirus. On the basis of the gross and histopathological findings, herpes simplex oesophagitis was diagnosed. After the patient completed a 10 day course of intravenous aciclovir, repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopies showed no abnormalities.
Herpes simplex virus is one of the most common pathogens causing infective oesophagitis. Herpes simplex oesophagitis is commonly seen in patients with immunosuppressive status, including after bone marrow transplantation, but has also been reported in immunocompetent individuals. In some patients, oesophagitis due to other pathogens such as cytomegalovirus or Candidia spp has been reported. Diagnosis is often confirmed by a combination of the gross oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings, a histopathological examination, and an immunohistochemical stain of the biopsied specimen. Oesophageal herpes simplex lesions detected by oesophagogastroduodenoscopy are typically referred to as volcano ulcers, and appear as discrete, diffusely scattered shallow ulcers. The Cowdry type-A inclusion body is a classic histopathological finding in biopsy specimens of herpes simplex oesopohagitis as seen in this case, and is observed in up to 70% of biopsy specimens.

A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease presented with fatigue, malaise, dizziness, difficulty ambulating, diarrhoea, easy bruising, and a diffuse rash involving her extremities and trunk that had been present for several days. She explained that she had limited her diet to consist mostly of bread, rice, dumplings, and the occasional egg white to reduce the symptoms she suffered from her gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Her diet was also devoid of red meat, fish, chicken, fruits, and vegetables.On physical examination, she had extensive, non-palpable, perifollicular haemorrhages involving her extremities (figure), ecchymosis (figure), and gingival bleeding. Corkscrew hairs, visible with the unaided eye, were seen all over her skin—although they were much more apparent with dermoscopy (figure). Her laboratory results showed haemoglobin 8·3 mg/dL, haematocrit 25·2%, and a plasma vitamin C concentration of <5 μmol/L (normal range 23–50 μmol/L). Endoscopy of the upper gastrointestinal tract and colonoscopy of the lower bowel did not find a source of bleeding.
A biopsy of the skin from her right lower leg showed a corkscrew shaped profile of the hair follicle, and histopathological examination showed follicular hyperkeratosis and plugging (figure). Taken together, the clinical, laboratory, and histopathological findings were consistent with a diagnosis of scurvy. Vitamin C must be obtained from dietary sources and it is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues for the synthesis of collagen. It is also important for immune system function and iron absorption. Scurvy rarely affects adults but may be seen in some individuals with malnutrition or malabsorption. Signs and symptoms usually occur by the third month of inadequate consumption, and treatment is with vitamin C supplementation. Early diagnosis and treatment of scurvy can be life-saving, so recognition of the physical findings is important. This patient was given intravenous vitamin C followed by daily oral supplementation and her symptoms resolved within a few weeks.

A 47-year-old woman presented to our institution with a 1-month history of swelling and a painless skin plaque on her left breast. 6 years earlier, the patient had been treated for luminal A invasive ductal carcinoma in the superomedial quadrant of the left breast; she had neoadjuvant chemotherapy, breast-conserving surgery, radiation therapy—a whole breast dose of 50 Gy plus a 10 Gy boost to the tumour bed—and oral tamoxifen. The patient had been found to have no recurrence of the tumour at any subsequent follow-up appointments. She had no history of breast trauma or lymphoedema.
On physical examination, we found the patient was generally well; she had a 1 cm purple plaque on the inferolateral quadrant of her left breast, approximately 1·5 cm from the areola (figure).Breast ultrasound examination showed skin thickening, subcutaneous oedema, and a predominantly hypoechoic nonmass finding in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast with irregular borders, regional distribution, and central hypervascularity on power Doppler (figure). Diagnostic mammogram showed a developing asymmetry in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast, as well as skin thickening and parenchymal oedema that were more pronounced compared with her previous mammograms (figure). Histological examination of a sample obtained by ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed solid epithelial proliferation with marked cellular atypia—initially deemed suspicious for recurrence of the carcinoma (figure). Immunohistochemistry results were positive for CD31, ERG, and D2-40 on most target cells and for CD34 in subgroups of target cells (appendix), along with very high Ki67 expression (90% of target cells), findings compatible with post radiation angiosarcoma.
On post-biopsy follow-up—54 days after the first ultrasound examination—the previously 1 cm wide skin lesion had progressed to a 4 cm irregular violaceous plaque with subtle areas of yellowish discoloration on adjacent skin (figure). On ultrasound examination, the lesion appeared as an irregular, hypoechoic mass with thick echogenic rind; the high central vascularity on power Doppler remained visible (appendix).
The findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options were discussed with the patient and together the decision was made to proceed to mastectomy of the affected breast.
On the day of mastectomy—60 days after the first ultrasound examination—additional satellite lesions and morphological changes in the nipple-areola complex were seen adjacent to the irregular violaceous plaque, with progression of the areas of yellowish skin discoloration (figure).
Histopathological analysis of a sample of the surgical specimen, which measured 9·0 cm × 7·0 cm X 6·0 cm and invaded the nipple, dermis, and parenchymal breast tissue, confirmed the diagnosis of post-radiation angiosarcoma. CT scans of the patient's head, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of metastases.
The patient made an uneventful recovery from the operation and was allowed home 24 h later. At follow-up 3 months after the mastectomy, a new 1 cm violaceous skin lesion surrounded by a yellowish halo appeared in the mastectomy scar (appendix); recurrence of the post-radiation angiosarcoma was confirmed by histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from surgically excised tissue.
Post-radiation angiosarcoma is an uncommon aggressive complication of radiotherapy for breast cancer, with a median latency period of 5–6 years. About one in every 1000 patients treated with radiotherapy for breast cancer may be at risk of developing the condition, and global incidence is expected to rise as the number of patients undergoing breast-preserving surgery plus radiotherapy increases. Typically, the tumour arises within the skin and subcutaneous tissues previously included in the irradiation field—this is unlike primary breast angiosarcomas which usually originate deep within the breast parenchyma. Patients with post-radiation angiosarcomas may develop breast swelling, erythema, skin thickening, and painless erythematous patches or plaques in previously irradiated areas, as well as areas of yellowish discoloration on circumjacent skin which is related to haemoglobin degradation products. Lymph node involvement is uncommon. Imaging findings, when present, are often non-specific and include skin and trabecular thickening, developing asymmetry on mammogram, and solid, irregular masses on breast ultrasound examination.
Surgical excision with negative margins is considered the standard treatment; prognosis is poor even with complete tumour resection, with 5-year survival rates of about 40%.

An 80-year-old man with a 1-week history of a red, swollen, and painful right leg presented to our emergency department. Additionally, he had reported long-term fatigue. A deep vein thrombosis was excluded after an ultrasound of his leg and he was found to have an infected ulcer caused by chronic venous insufficiency and an iron deficiency anaemia. The patient was referred to our clinic for further exploration of his anaemia and painful leg.He had previously had a coronary artery bypass graft; he had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; atherosclerosis with peripheral arterial occlusive disease and coronary artery disease; recurrent deep venous thromboses; and alcohol misuse.
Laboratory investigations had previously found a low haemoglobin concentration of 9·8 g/dL (typical range 13·7–17·7), a mean corpuscular volume of 91 fL (typical range 80–100), and a serum ferritin concentration of 17 μg/L (typical range 22–320).
On examination we found the patient to be pale but not acute unwell. He had ulcers and pitting oedema of both shins and soft respiratory sounds in both lung bases.
Ordinarily, we would have done a routine colonoscopy to investigate possible causes of the patient's anaemia. However, considering the patient's general health and the likelihood of proceeding to surgery being low, we decided to manage the case conservatively.
An abdominal CT showed an unexplained lesion about 6·1 cm in length, located near the xiphoid, ventral to the liver (figure). No other atypical findings were seen. On review of a previous scan, done 4 years earlier, we found that the lesion had been present for some time and that it had increased in size.
Histopathological examination of a sample from a biopsy of the lesion showed lipocytes, megakaryocytes, erythroid precursors, and myeloid precursors: indicative of extramedullary haematopoiesis (EMH; figure).
Additional laboratory investigations ruled out monoclonal proliferation of plasma cells—no M-protein was detectable and no JAK2 gene mutation was found. We did not do a bone marrow aspiration, for the reason stated above regarding the colonoscopy.
After 2 weeks of treating his ulcers with clindamycin and 2 months of ferrous fumarate, his haemoglobin concentration was 17·7 g/dL and his shins had improved.
Considering all the patient's pathologies, we believe that the cause of the EMH was likely to be multifactorial: the chronic ulcers and atherosclerosis, and the iron deficiency anaemia.
EMH is the expansion and differentiation of haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells outside the bone marrow as a compensatory mechanism for ineffective haematopoiesis. In adults, EMH typically occurs in the presence of myeloproliferative malignancies. That it is also associated with other conditions—including thalassemia—is well appreciated.
Sites commonly affected are the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes; paravertebral areas, heart, chest, thymus, kidney, adrenal gland, prostate, pleura, nerves in the skin and spinal canal may be involved, but less frequently. On discovering a site of EMH, extensive investigations should be made to find the cause; appropriate treatment can then be started.
EMH in unusual locations—as seen in our patient—needs regular monitoring, and in selected cases where the lesion is causing local symptoms, surgical resection might be considered; not a realistic possibility in this case.
options: Lung, Spleen, Heart, Mediastinum

input:
A 64-year-old woman was referred to our department because of weakness and dizziness that had been troubling her for 3 weeks. She had a microcytic anaemia as noted by her primary care physician: her full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·6 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume of 62·4 fL (normal range 77–95). She said she had never had a period and she did not know why; she had never received any treatment for this problem.Physical examination showed that the patient was short in stature (1·54 m), and that the fourth digit—ring finger—on her left hand (figure) and the fourth digits on both her feet were also noticeably short (figure). She was also partly deaf. According to her medical history, she had hypertension, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, scoliosis, and osteoporosis, and had a recent compression fracture of her L2 vertebra; she had been taking diclofenac 75 mg once or twice a day for several weeks, depending on the intensity of the pain in her back.
We confirmed the patient was iron deficient: her serum iron concentration was 3·4 μmol/L (normal range 10·7–32·2), transferrin saturation was 3% (normal range 16–45), and faecal occult blood (FOB) tests were positive. We did a gastroscopy, which showed an ulcer in the gastric antrum and erosions in the fornix; a colonoscopy showed no abnormalities. We started her on treatment with pantoprazole 40 mg twice a day, and 10 days later FOB tests were negative. Serology testing for coeliac disease was negative and there were no signs of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) at endoscopy.
Considering the patient's physical signs and medical history, we suspected that she had Turner syndrome. An x-ray of her hands clearly showed a shortened left fourth metacarpal (figure) and Madelung deformity—an abnormality arising from premature arrest of growth along the medial volar aspect of the distal radius—of her left wrist, both characteristic of Turner syndrome. The diagnosis was confirmed by karyotyping, which showed the patient to have a 45,X karyotype (figure). Interestingly, 2 weeks after admission, the patient's relatives presented us with a karyotyping report dated 1980, which also showed X monosomy. We believe that the endoscopic findings and improvement after treatment with the proton pump inhibitor indicate that gastric mucosa damage was responsible for our patient's anaemia. Further, we surmise chronic low levels of oestrogen—the result of many years of no treatment—resulted in her severe osteoporosis and back pains, and prolonged use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to treat the pain then caused the gastropathy and blood loss (video).
Turner syndrome is a rare condition in women and is characterised by complete or partial loss of one X chromosome. Patients are short in stature and have ovarian dysgenesis which leads to sexual infantilism, amenorrhoea, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, and endocrine and metabolic disorders. They are at increased risk of autoimmune disorders. With regards to gastrointestinal diseases, the syndrome is associated with coeliac disease, IBD, and intestinal angiodysplasia—all of which can cause iron deficiency anaemia.
Best practice and care for Turner syndrome require a multidisciplinary approach and seeing the patient regularly throughout her life.

options: Coeliac disease serology, Faecal occult bloods, Oral iron absorption test, All the above

A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with fevers and chills in December, 2014, and was admitted with a diagnosis of pneumonia. CT to exclude pulmonary embolus showed diffuse osseous lytic lesions, and he was also found to have anaemia and an IgG kappa monoclonal protein of 55·8 g/L on protein electrophoresis (a single band). After a bone marrow biopsy he was given a diagnosis of plasma cell myeloma and was treated with four cycles of CyBorD chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone) in preparation for an autologous stem cell transplantation.
The aspirate from the bone marrow sampling showed a substantial increase in plasma cells (figure). The bone marrow core biopsy sample showed a hypercellular marrow with increased plasma cells, estimated to occupy 80% of marrow cellularity by CD138 immunohistochemistry. We saw that the neoplastic plasma cells had two distinct immunophenotypes: one population expressed CD138, kappa, and CD56; the other expressed CD138, kappa, CD20, and CD79a. Morphological differences were visible on routine haematoxylin and eosin staining, with prominent nucleoli in the CD56 area (figure). We could not create a more extensive immunophenotype because of tissue limitations, and too few events were captured by flow cytometry to allow characterisation using this technique.
options: Langerhans cell histiocytosis, Acute basophilic leukemia, Plasma cell myeloma, Systemic mastocytosis

input:
A 51-year-old woman attended our emergency department with a 3-day history of dyspnoea, fatigue, and cough; 11 days earlier she had the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccination. On examination she was afebrile, her peripheral oxygen saturation was 98% (fraction of inspired O2 21%), blood pressure was 150/90 mm Hg, heart rate was 98 beats per min, and body-mass index was 31 kg/m2.Laboratory investigations showed a severe thrombocytopenia of 37 × 109 platelets per L; 3 days earlier it had been 178 × 109 per L (normal 140–440). Serum concentrations of D-dimer (>34 mg/dL; normal <0·5) and C-reactive protein were increased (42 mg/L; normal <0·5); prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, fibrinogen, creatinine, electrolytes, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and high-sensitivity troponin T were within normal range. SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab was negative.
CT pulmonary angiography showed a central pulmonary embolism without right ventricular dysfunction (figure). Magnetic resonance venography showed venous thrombus formation in the left internal iliac vein—including the common iliac vein—with extension into the inferior vena cava (figure; appendix).
We started low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH) at half the therapeutic dose. The patient was admitted and empirically treated with dexamethasone 40 mg orally—we assumed an autoimmune process was responsible for the rapid platelet reduction. Other causes of thrombocytopenia were excluded (appendix).
After 3 days of glucocorticoid therapy, the patient's platelet concentration remained low and the fibrinogen levels dropped rapidly to below 50 mg/dL; factor XIII also dropped to 32% activity (normal >70%); the prothrombin time became unmeasurable. Plasma coagulation factor activities were normal for all other extrinsic and intrinsic coagulation factors—including von Willebrand factor.
Mixing the patient's plasma in a 1:1 ratio with standard human plasma showed a deficiency of fibrinogen and factor XIII; thrombelastography confirmed the result (for details see appendix).
LMWH was increased to a therapeutic dose leading to an anti-factor Xa activity of 0·5–1·0 IU/mL (therapeutic range 0·5–1·0).
On day 5, the patient developed pain in the left lower back and left gluteal region; CT venography showed an increase in the thrombus in the inferior vena cava. The LMWH dose was increased to obtain supratherapeutic anti-factor Xa activity (1·0–1·5 U/mL). On the following day, the pain had reduced.
Over the next 7 days, the platelet count and factor XIII activity increased; fibrinogen levels also started to increase after the platelet count reached 100 × 109 per L. 11 days after admission the platelet count was 173 × 109 per L, fibrinogen concentration was 228 mg/L, and factor XIII activity was 78% (appendix). Anticoagulation therapy was switched from LMWH to oral dabigatran 150 mg twice a day and on day 15 the patient was well and allowed home.
Activation of the coagulation system producing thromboses in the context of thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinogenaemia—as occurred in our patient—is similar to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and to that seen in critically ill COVID-19 patients (video).

input: A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 1-month history of dizziness and episodes of hypotension during his outpatient haemodialysis sessions. In addition to end-stage renal disease, the patient had a history of a large anterior myocardial infarction and subsequent percutaneous coronary interventions with stent placement; this had resulted in an ischaemic cardiomyopathy, which had required the implantation of a left ventricular assist device 5 years before this admission. On examination, the patient had a distended jugular vein, a pulsatile liver, and prominent, pulsating facial veins (figure, video 1). An echocardiogram showed severe tricuspid regurgitation that was caused by annular dilatation and this, in turn, had resulted in malcoaptation of the valve leaflets (video 2). The patient was also noted to have significant enlargement and dysfunction of the right ventricle, as well as diastolic septal shift, indicating volume overload of the right ventricle (video 2). Ventricularisation of the right atrial pressure tracing—with C-V waves that indicated severe tricuspid regurgitation—was seen during cardiac catheterisation. Despite treatment with intravenous ionotropes, the patient's right ventricular failure worsened and, sadly, he died in a hospice, 6 weeks after he first came to see us.Right ventricular failure after left ventricular assist device implantation is unfortunately common and results in significant morbidity and mortality. It is important to be able to recognise both the common features—such as jugular vein distension and a pulsatile liver—and the rare features, such as pulsation of the facial vein, in the diagnosis of right ventricular failure with concomitant tricuspid regurgitation. Renowned Scottish cardiologist Sir James Mackenzie was one of the first physicians to publish a detailed description of pulsation of the facial vein associated with tricuspid regurgitation, in 1892, and the phenomenon has been the subject of much debate since then. Transmission of atrial pulsations to the facial vein are usually prevented by venous valves present around the lower border of the mandible and in the jugular venous system. However, incompetence—and even complete absence—of these valves has been reported in patients with longstanding tricuspid regurgitation and elevated central venous pressure.
options: Arteriovenous fistula, Corrigan’s pulse from aortic regurgitation, De Musset’s sign due to aortic regurgitation, Severe tricuspid regurgitation

input:
A 32-year-old right-handed woman presented to our neurology clinic with a 3-month history of intermittent blurriness of her vision and left-sided paraesthesia in her arm and leg. The patient said the problems began shortly after she gave birth to her first child and gradually became worse over the following 12 weeks.She had no significant medical history and was prescribed no medications.
On examination she was fit and well; she had no retinal hemangiomas, her hearing was normal, and we found no neurofibromas. A full neurological review found no abnormalities: specifically, her visual acuity was unaffected; a sensory system and cerebellar examination were within normal limits. Notably, the patient's left-sided paraesthesia did not follow a dermatomal distribution.
All laboratory investigations—including the haematocrit—were normal. We did not carry out any genetic testing.
An MRI of the patient's brain showed a 3 mm lesion within the inferior aspect of the posterior lobe of the left cerebellum; the lesion demonstrated contrast enhancement on T1 weighted imaging (figure), suggesting vascularity. A digital subtraction angiogram showed no evidence of a shunting vascular malformation. We were unable to make a clear diagnosis at that time because the MRI findings did not correlate with the patient's symptoms. We therefore decided to observe the lesion with repeated imaging over an extended period of follow-up. At the time, our list of initial differential diagnoses included vascular lesions, such as arteriovenous malformations, metastatic tumour, and primary cerebellar tumour.
2 years later, the abnormality had grown to 5 mm at its widest part (figure) and was surrounded by a small amount of oedema. Importantly, the patient reported no change in her symptomatology and had no abnormalities on neurological examination. We decided to continue watching and waiting: monitoring the lesion with radiographic imaging and follow-up appointments. The possibility of resection was discussed with the patient but she decided to continue with the plan to keep the situation under observation and review.
4 years after initial presentation, an expansile intraparenchymal fluid collection had developed around the lesion, which now had the characteristic appearance of a cerebellar hemangioblastoma (figure); the pathognomonic findings included a T2 hyperintense cyst with a non-enhancing wall and a strongly enhancing mural nodule.
The patient elected to have a suboccipital craniotomy in order to remove the lesion; intraoperative findings were consistent with a hemangioblastoma and the procedure was completed without any complications. She recovered fully from the operation and at follow-up 2 years later, she was neurologically intact and reported resolution of her initial presenting symptoms.
The relationship between pregnancy and its potentiation of cerebellar hemangioblastoma formation continues to cause controversy. Our case—where the patient presented shortly after giving birth without a clear association between her presenting symptoms and the initial MRI findings—unfortunately prevented us from adding any significant insights into the debate.
In addition, while the majority of cerebellar hemangioblastomas are associated with Von Hippel–Lindau disease, some, like our patient, lack the other characteristic features of the syndrome: angiomatosis including retinal capillary hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts and tumours, and endolymphatic sac tumours (video).
options: Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Von Hippel-Lindau disease, Sturge-Weber syndrome, Neurofibromatosis Type 2

input:
A 58-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent fever and pancytopenia. Physical examination showed no other abnormal findings. However, a septic screen isolated Mycobacterium abscessus from his blood and bone marrow. An 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an area of increased uptake in the patient's prostate (figure). Prostate specific antigen was 8·06 ng/mL—previously, it had been measured and reported to be 0·8 ng/mL. A transrectal biopsy of his prostate showed granulomatous inflammation. Tissue cultures grew M abscessus. He said he had never had prostatic manipulation before. However, he had been previously diagnosed with benign prostatic enlargement and, 1 year before start of current symptoms, he had surgical resection of a neuroendocrine intestinal tumour.Recently, despite no evidence of residual disease, he had become worried about the possibility of recurrence. He decided to respond to an advertisement he had heard on the radio extolling the benefits of stem cell treatments—including cancer prevention or recurrence. He said the clinic told him that the treatment was a type of “immunotherapy” that would allow his own stem cells to recognise any cancer cells as abnormal and destroy them. Further, he said they explained that the procedure entailed extracting his blood which would then be “stimulated to produce abundant stem cells” and these would then be injected into him intravenously.
A few hours after the infusion, the patient developed profuse vomiting and high-grade fever. He was given intravenous hydration and antibiotics, without resolution. He then attended our hospital.
Initially, we ruled out immunodeficiency—a hallmark of disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacteria—and only after repeat questioning of other possible risk factors did he disclose details of the “stem cell treatment”. We believe the “stem cells” had been contaminated with mycobacteria prior to being transfused into the patient. The infusion—into the blood stream—enabled dissemination and seeding of the mycobacteria in the previously diseased prostate.
The field of stem cell therapy has grown substantially. However, unregulated, unscientifically proven, and irresponsible use has also increased worldwide leading to rising numbers of cases of patients being infected from products contaminated with a variety of different bacteria including Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter cloacae, and Citrobacter freundii.
options: Disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease, Prostatic carcinoma, Pseudomonal prostatitis, Primary prostatic lymphoma

input:
A 53-year-old man was referred to the dermatology clinic with a 20-year history of a generalised, pruritic rash—with features of both psoriasis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis—and an 8-year history of progressive arthritis, diagnosed as polyarticular gout, that had recently affected his ability to walk.The patient had been prescribed topical steroids and allopurinol with little improvement to his skin or joint disease.
On examination he was generally well but confined to a gurney because of his arthritis. He had ill-defined facial erythema and erythematous scaly plaques involving approximately 30% of the body surface area of his trunk and extremities (figure; appendix). He also had tophaceous nodules and flexion deformities bilaterally in both his metacarpophalangeal and proximal inter-phalangeal joints.
While the patient's thin, scaly lesions resembled an eczematous dermatitis, the moderate demarcation of some plaques suggested psoriatic skin disease, so he was initiated on the tumour necrosis factor-α (TNFα) inhibitor adalimumab; no improvement was noted at 5 months and it was stopped (appendix).
Histopathological examination of a sample of a skin biopsy—with the hope of clarifying the diagnosis—showed the spongiotic pattern of an eczematous dermatitis (appendix). The anti-interleukin-4 receptor (IL-4R) α antibody, dupilumab—approved for eczema in the form of atopic dermatitis—was prescribed which, after 5 months, failed to show any clinical improvement.
To gain further understanding of our patient's disease, a single-cell RNA sequencing profile of his skin-resident T cells was performed—part of an ongoing molecular study of complex cases of skin disease (appendix). The skin T-cell transcriptomes closely resembled those of classic psoriasis, rather than atopic dermatitis (one-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test, W=56, p=0·0002; figure); they also showed elevated IL-23 pathway transcripts which included Chimerin 1 and Cathepsin H. Therefore, the patient was initiated on the IL-23 inhibitor, tildrakizumab, considered to be more specific for the treatment of psoriasis. Significant clearance of the patient's skin plaques was noted after 16 weeks, which was sustained at follow-up 9 months later (figure; appendix). The patient also reported substantial improvement in joint mobility and regained his ability to walk independently and to type on a keyboard. Therefore, we believe that in addition to gout, the patient had long-standing, undiagnosed psoriatic joint disease, which was improved by IL-23 blockade. Further, since the two forms of joint disease are known to co-occur, they may have arisen from a common pathway abnormality.
Overactivity of the IL-23 signalling pathway is involved in a range of skin diseases, including psoriasis vulgaris, some cases of pityriasis rubra pilaris, and hidradenitis suppurativa. TNFα inhibitors are effective in approximately 60% of psoriasis patients; treating empirically with these medications—particularly in non-classic clinical presentations—provides limited diagnostic information. In eczematous rashes with psoriasiform features, it is important to consider the possibility of IL-23-driven diatheses, which may cause both cutaneous and joint disease. Using high-resolution transcriptomic analysis may—as in this case with indistinct clinical features—enable more precise targeting of treatments in patients with a broad range of chronic inflammatory conditions.
options: IL-1A, IL-17A, IL-13, IL-31

input: A 10-year-old boy, 144 cm tall, was referred to our hospital in October, 2012, with a 2 month history of persistent pain in the buttocks. He had altered gait due to pain, but no disturbance of bladder or bowels. Radiographs, CT, and MRI showed a large osteolytic lesion in the sacrum, and examination of a bone biopsy sample confirmed a giant cell tumour of bone, which we considered to be unresectable because of the potential risk of neurological deficit and massive bleeding. We obtained informed consent from the patient and his parents and the review board for off-label use of denosumab, a potent inhibitor of osteoclastic bone resorption, to reduce the tumour mass. We gave subcutaneous denosumab 120 mg every 4 weeks, with loading doses on days 8 and 15 of the first cycle. Due to the excellent clinical response and the obvious sclerotic changes along the growth plates (figure) we stopped treatment after five cycles (seven injections). The sclerosing bands were seen in almost all the radiographs of metaphyses, most prominently in the distal radius and ulna, and also in the proximal humerus, proximal femur, and phalanges of the fingers. During the 5 months off treatment the tumour grew again, so we restarted treatment with denosumab for 4 months until the tumour had reduced enough in size for surgery to be safely carried out. Before surgery repeat radiographs showed double-layered sclerotic bands at the metaphysis (figure), reflecting the longitudinal bone growth during the periods on and off denosumab. At last follow-up in March, 2014, the patient showed no signs of growth retardation (151 cm tall), was able to participate in sports without pain, and showed no evidence of tumour recurrence.
options: Juvenile Paget's disease, Hyperparathyroidism, Bone infarction, Bone-modifying agents

input:
A newborn baby girl with blueish-coloured skin lesions on the tips of the first, second, and fourth toes of her right foot was brought to our unit 12 h after birth (figure). Apart from the noted abnormalities, the patient was healthy; she was normally alert and showing no clinical signs of pain. The respiratory rate was between 40 and 50 breaths per min, oxygen saturation was over 95% on room air, heart rate was between 120 and 140 beats per min, and temperature was 36·5°C. No history of mechanical or physical damage and no familial predisposition to thromboembolic events or autoimmune diseases was reported.Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood count, coagulation studies, and infection parameters—including C-reactive protein concentration (0·13 mg/dL; normal <0·5) and interleukin-6 concentration (18·6 ng/L; normal <50). The day after presentation, the lesions evolved into acral necrosis.
The baby's mother reported infection with SARS-CoV-2 in mid-pregnancy with mild COVID-19 symptoms of a cough, rhinitis, aching limbs, and a sore throat. Serological testing of neonatal serum collected on the sixth day of the baby's life showed an anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibody concentration against spike protein S1 receptor-binding domain of 766 U/mL. Neonatal RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.
At this stage, our working diagnosis was acral gangrenous necrosis following a thromboembolic event. We decided to manage the case conservatively with the use of dry dressings; one month after the lesions’ appearance, they were healing spontaneously apart from a small crust on the tip of the first toe (figure).
Blue toe syndrome is well described in adults; one or more of the toes become blue or purple, due to decreased arterial flow, impaired venous outflow, and abnormal circulating blood. Specific causes are numerous, and identification depends upon methodical history taking, a complete physical examination, and selected laboratory investigations.
In neonates, blue toe syndrome is mostly a benign condition, related to acrocyanosis caused by peripheral vasoconstriction and increased tissue oxygen extraction. Newborn infants are the most vulnerable group of paediatric patients likely to develop thrombosis and have thromboembolic complications. Pathological processes in the placenta—associated with maternal infections—might be important in the aetiology. Neonatal vascular complications have been reported following intrauterine SARS-CoV-2 exposure and might be caused by a hypercoagulable state in the fetus. In our case, the prepartum SARS-CoV-2 infection was possibly related to the patient's blue toes. However, because the maternal infection occurred several months prior to birth, there was no evidence of the neonate being infected, and coagulation tests were all within normal range, it seems unlikely.
output: The condition is mostly benign, related to acrocyanosis
target: The condition is mostly benign, related to acrocyanosis
options: The condition usually resolves within 2-3 h, The condition is mostly benign, related to acrocyanosis, Surgical removal of the toes is the only therapeutic option, The cause is usually thromboembolic events of maternal origin

input:
A previously healthy 6-month-old male infant was brought to an external dermatology clinic on March 24, 2017, with an eruption of non-tender and non-pruritic vesicles and blisters over his truncal region that had appeared within the previous month. He was subsequently referred to the Pediatric Dermatology Unit at KK Women's and Children's Hospital, Singapore, for evaluation and investigations. The patient had no preceding or intercurrent illness, nor any positive contact or travel history. His only notable family history was atopic dermatitis in his mother and brother. On physical examination, there were several small vesicles and large blisters filled with clear fluid distributed over the back and gluteal region (figure, A). Some of the vesicles and blisters had resolved spontaneously, with residual scaly erythematous plaques and papules. The face and extremities were not involved.A punch biopsy over the residual plaques showed a mixed inflammatory infiltrate in the superficial dermis consisting primarily of large histiocytic cells with kidney-shaped nuclei and abundant light pinkish cytoplasm. These cells were also seen in small vacuoles in all levels of the epidermis, and stained positively for CD1a, S100, and Langerin (CD207) immunohistochemical stains (figure, B). The BRAFV600E immunohistochemical stain was positive, indicating a mutation in the gene. Admixed eosinophils and lymphocytes were present within the dermal infiltrate. A diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis was made on clinical-pathological correlation. A full blood count, skeletal survey, ultrasound of the hepatobiliary system, liver function test, and microscopic urinalysis did not reveal any extra-cutaneous manifestations of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Treatment was started with mometasone furoate 0·1% topical cream twice daily. After 3 months, there was significant clinical improvement and resolution of the lesions.
Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a rare disease characterised by the aberrant clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells. The gold standard for diagnosis of this condition is through histological and immunohistochemical diagnosis, with positivity of CD1a, Langerin (CD207), or both in the lesion. Skin involvement of Langerhans cell histiocytosis is seen in about 40% of patients, commonly as an eczematous rash and ulcerative lesions. However, manifestation of cutaneous Langerhans cell histiocytosis in the form of a vesicular or bullous subtype is rare.
Treatment with topical steroids seemed to be effective in this young patient with blistering cutaneous Langerhans cell histiocytosis. We will continue to monitor him closely for cutaneous recurrences and evolution to systemic involvements in the future. Other therapies that have previously been reported to be effective for non-blistering Langerhans cell histiocytosis, including topical nitrogen mustard, psoralen with ultraviolet therapy and topical tacrolimus, might also be explored as alternatives in the treatment of blistering Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

A 44-year-old night porter presented to our clinic with difficulty walking, instability, and stiffness—particularly in the muscles of his face—which had developed over the previous 3 weeks. His wife said that he had also been tired and lethargic for about 1 year.He had been seen in our hepatology outpatient clinic 12 months earlier because of a raised aspartate aminotransaminase (AST) of 43 IU/L (normal 11–34) and gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) of 301 IU/L (normal 12–68); his alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and bilirubin were normal. Investigations showed no evidence of active viral hepatitis, haemochromatosis, α1 antitrypsin deficiency, or autoimmune liver disease. Serum ceruloplasmin concentration was reduced at 0·11 g/L (normal 0·2–0·6). Ultrasound and transient elastography showed signs of fibrosis and a liver biopsy specimen showed microvesicular steatosis, bilirubinostasis, and severe fibrosis with incomplete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was negative. The patient's mother had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease at age 70 years (see appendix for full family tree).
On examination we found him to have symmetrical cog-wheel muscle rigidity and hypokinetic movements bilaterally. He had diminished arm swing, he was unstable, and when he walked he episodically had short, accelerating steps. He had a mask-like facial expression with a fixed smile—risus sardonicus (figure; video). Investigations found an AST of 128 IU/L, ALT of 131 IU/L, GGT of 497 IU/L, and bilirubin of 64·4 μmol/L (normal <24).
The patient's symptoms deteriorated significantly over the following weeks: he was barely able to walk, he was bradykinetic with episodes of freezing, and he was very unstable on his feet (video). A single photon emission CT DaTSCAN (GE Healthcare, Amersham, UK), 5 weeks after his symptoms began, showed bilaterally reduced presynaptic dopamine transporter in the striatum (figure). Slit-lamp examination of his eyes was normal. The patient's serum ceruloplasmin concentration was again low 0·13 g/L and his urine copper excretion was markedly increased at 5·81 μmol per 24 h (normal <0·95). Histological examination of a biopsy specimen of his liver showed severe progressive chronic hepatitis with cholestasis and fibrosis with complete cirrhosis. Rhodanine staining for copper was again negative. However, analysis using atomic absorption spectrometry showed increased hepatic copper concentrations of 325 μg/g (normal 10–35). We confirmed a diagnosis of Wilson's disease by DNA sequencing, which showed that the patient was homozygous for a missense variant of the ATP7B, gene 2998G →A leading to Gly1000Arg substitution.
We started chelation therapy—8 weeks after his neurological symptoms began—with penicillamine. However, the patient's extrapyramidal motor symptoms worsened—probably because of mobilisation of the excess copper and deposition into the basal ganglia. So we switched penicillamine to trientine. The patient's symptoms—apart from the risus sardonicus—showed considerable improvement after 5 months of treatment.
Wilson's disease is an important and treatable differential diagnosis of rapidly developing extra-pyramidal or atypical Parkinsonian symptoms. Even if the patient is over 40 years of age, there are no eye signs—eg Kayser-Fleischer rings, or sunflower cataracts, and conventional histopathological analysis of a liver biopsy with rhodanine stain was negative.

A 67-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of a low-grade fever and progressive weakness in the muscles of his face. He also reported drooling and slurred speech.He had a 10-year history of hypertension that was treated with antihypertensives.
On examination we found that he could not close his eyes, wrinkle his forehead, or raise his eyebrows and that the nasolabial folds of his face were flattened—indicating a bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (figure). We found no other abnormalities on physical examination.
Laboratory investigations showed a mild anaemia, with a haemoglobin concentration of 11·6 g/dL, a leucocytosis of 17·2 × 109 per L, and a monocytosis of 2·14 × 109 per L. The patient's erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 10 mg/L. Infectious diseases—including Lyme disease, HIV, syphilis, and herpes zoster—were excluded. Neoplasms—particularly head and neck tumours—were ruled out, and granulomatous diseases, like sarcoidosis, and metabolic and autoimmune diseases—including Guillain–Barré syndrome, systemic autoimmune diseases, and vasculitis were excluded.
A peripheral blood smear showed excessive monocytosis with left shift, dysplastic granulocytes, promonocytes, and blasts (figure). A bone marrow aspiration confirmed the diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML).
Cytogenetic analysis found trisomy of chromosome 8; DNA sequencing showed mutations in the RUNX1, SF3B1, and CBL genes. Nerve conduction studies found an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy—affecting the facial nerves and the peripheral nerves in the patient's arms and legs. We decided to treat the patient using corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. He remained afebrile with no improvement of his facial nerve palsy. We decided against using hypomethylating agents because in Europe azacitidine has been approved only for CMML patients with white blood cell counts of less than 13 × 109 per L.
2 months later, while still on steroid therapy, the patient was admitted with a fever, aphthous stomatitis, and arthralgias. Physical examination found an aphthous ulceration on the right side of the tongue, synovitis of the wrists and right knee, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Soon after admission, the patient complained of an acute onset abdominal pain; he was hypotensive and tachycardic, and had tenderness and rigidity of the right upper quadrant. Multiphase CT scan of the abdomen showed a large haematoma of the right kidney with active bleeding; he also had multiple disseminated microaneurysms—up to 1 cm in diameter—of both interlobar arteries, indicative of a medium-vessel vasculitis (figure). He underwent urgent right radical nephrectomy.
Histology showed a focal necrotising arteritis with mixed inflammatory infiltration and fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel walls and intramural thrombosis of medium-size vessels—resembling polyarteritis nodosa. We decided to start him on cyclophosphamide and continue with the steroids: this led to a significant decline of acute phase reactants. 10 days later, an aneurysm in the remaining kidney ruptured and we had to do a further radical nephrectomy, resulting in the patient requiring haemodialysis. However, 3 weeks after the cyclophosphamide was started, we noted a significant improvement in his facial nerve palsies.
CMML is a myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative neoplasm, sometimes associated with extrahaematological manifestations: autoimmune inflammatory phenomena can cause a systemic vasculitis, connective tissue diseases, relapsing polychondritis, and a seronegative arthritis. High clinical suspicion for such atypical manifestations should be considered in all patients with CMML (video).

input: A 38-year-old man presented to the First Department of Orthopaedics at the University of Athens in June, 2013, with a 4-year history of an enlarging left shoulder mass. He reported minor recurrent injury during athletic activity. Medical and family history were unremarkable. Clinical examination showed a firm, painless mass. Radiography showed calcifications posterior to the left scapula (figure, A). CT scan showed multiple calcified nodules, without scapular erosion (figure, B). MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity (figure, C). Serum calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, and amounts of parathyroid hormone were within normal limits. Differential diagnosis included tumoral calcinosis, myositis ossificans, synovial chondromatosis, and synovial sarcoma. Tumoral calcinosis consists of lobulated, well-demarked calcifications, generally at the extensor surfaces of large joints. Myositis ossificans consists of bone and cartilage formation within muscle; rapid evolution and absence of lobular morphology are typical features. Synovial chondromatosis consists of intrasynovial proliferation of cartilage, with typical rings-and-arcs calcifications and intra-articular location. Synovial sarcomas are poorly defined and infiltrative, with punctuate calcifications occurring sporadically. Because of the absence of family history of tumoral calcinosis and biochemical abnormalities in this patient, and to avoid potential diagnostic pitfalls, a needle biopsy was done. Histology was consistent with tumoral calcinosis showing amorphous calcium nodules surrounded by histiocytic and giant cell reaction. The lesion was completely surgically excised, without any recurrence at the 3-year follow-up in September, 2016. Follow-up is ongoing.

A 75-year-old man presented with a 12-month history of increasing pain in his right knee; he said that intermittently he had “popping” sensations and episodic locking of the joint that prevented full extension. The patient also reported feeling like objects were moving inside his knee; 10 years earlier, he had a partial medial meniscectomy on the same knee. In addition, the patient reported that 3 years before, he had similar transient symptoms in his left knee; an MRI at that time had shown a loose body of similar signal intensity to bone and cartilage in proton density-weighted spectral attenuated inversion-recovery sequences (figure).On examination, we found the patient to be generally well. He had a 10 degree (normal 0) fixed flexion deformity of the right knee with full flexion limited to 100 degrees (normal 135).
X-rays showed popcorn-shaped loose bodies in the supra-patellar pouch and osteoarthritis in the knee, consistent with synovial osteochondromatosis (figure).
A total right knee replacement was done because of the extent of the osteoarthritis in the joint; intra-operatively the loose bodies were removed (figure).
Postoperatively, the patient's pain and function of his right knee had significantly improved. At follow-up 18 months later, his function was normal with a range of movements from 0 to 120 degrees and his pain had resolved.
Pseudo-locking of the knee occurs when pain inhibits movement of the joint; this can be caused by pain from trauma, arthritis, inflammatory conditions, and abnormalities of the patella. Mechanical locking, which is also known as true locking, results from a physical block to full extension of the knee, which most frequently results from a meniscal tear of a loose body in the joint. Loose bodies can be cartilaginous or osseous.
Synovial osteochondromatosis is predominantly a benign condition which occurs when foci of synovium undergo metaplasia into cartilage-producing tissue. The metaplastic nidus produces sessile nodules which may ossify but ultimately bud off into the joint, forming loose bodies. When ossified, they are radio-opaque and display a characteristic popcorn appearance. The diagnosis can typically be made on plain x-rays; on MRI they appear as loose bodies of a similar signal to cartilage. Histologically, the condition is characterised by multiple hyaline cartilage nodules within the synovium. Nodules that have budded off from the synovium may cause third-body wear which accelerates and aggravates arthritis. They may also cause the mechanical symptom of locking. The condition can affect any joint, but the knee is the most common.
Treatment involves arthroscopic retrieval or total joint replacement in cases with concomitant osteoarthritis. Notably, malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma is very rare.

A 52-year-old man attended our hospital reporting breathlessness on exertion that had been worsening over the past 2 weeks. He had smoked 20 cigarettes a day for the past 40 years. He had no other symptoms—specifically no systemic or gastrointestinal complaints. The patient had tried to quit smoking 4 months earlier and had started vaping: he had been using commercially available e-cigarettes which did not have any Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) added.The symptoms started some days after the patient had added a new flavour—blueberry—to the vaping fluid.
On examination, we found the patient to be apyrexial, with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg, a heart rate of 70 beats per min, and in sinus rhythm. Auscultation of his chest found no heart murmurs, but we heard vesicular breath sounds with discrete bilateral crepitations over the lung bases.
A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest (figure) showed lower lobe predominant, bilateral consolidations in a peribronchovascular distribution—the pattern of organising pneumonia. Extensive diagnostic work-up did not provide any evidence for an infectious or rheumatological aetiology: C-reactive protein concentration and leucocyte count were normal. Antibody screening for hypersensitivity pneumonitis and collagen vascular disease was negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for any pathogenic agents; however, it showed a lymphocytic alveolitis with 70% lymphocytes.
Histopathological examination of a transbronchial lung biopsy confirmed an organising pneumonia, with interspersed pigment-containing macrophages indicating foreign body inhalation.
The patient stopped vaping e-cigarettes and was prescribed systemic steroid therapy, starting with 40 mg of oral prednisolone per day for 4 weeks, reducing by 10 mg per day every 4 weeks—he is currently on 10 mg per day. After 4 months there was no improvement in the patient's symptoms and the imaging findings remained unchanged. 6 months after he first presented, we repeated the bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and cryobiopsy: we found no signs of lymphocytic alveolitis, but histopathology reported a diagnosis of non-specific interstitial pneumonia. We concluded the patient had e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) that had taken a chronic course—starting with the organising pneumonia and evolving into a fibrosing non-specific interstitial pneumonia. Most cases of EVALI reported in the literature have involved patients using e-cigarettes with THC or cannabidiol added to the vaping liquid, where vitamin E is thought to be important in causing the lung damage; however, concerns about the effects of the constituents of the flavourings have also been raised. EVALI cases comprise heterogeneous lung pathologies including acute eosinophilic pneumonia, diffuse alveolar damage and acute respiratory distress syndrome, and—as we initially found in our case—an organising pneumonia (video).
options: Diffuse alveolar damage, Acute eosinophilic pneumonia, Usual interstitial pneumonia, Organising pneumonia

The case of Mary Mallon, an asymptomatic carrier who infected 51 people while working as a cook and laundress in New York in 1906–15, showed that Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S Typhi) is able to lurk in the gallbladder without overt clinical signs and spread enteric fever through person-to-person transmission.
In May, 2009, a 42-year-old man presented to Patan Hospital in Kathmandu, Nepal, with acute, sudden, severe pain in his right upper quadrant lasting for 2 days. We diagnosed cholecystitis and he underwent a cholecystectomy and made a prompt recovery. S Typhi was cultured from the bile in his gallbladder, and the cholecystitis was confirmed histologically.
We used immunofluorescent labelling to analyse a section of his gallbladder with a confocal microscope (figure). Initially, we bound primary antibody (O9; Murex, Dartford, UK) to the cellular (bacterial) antigen, which was then specifically bound to a secondary fluorochrome-conjugated antibody. The 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) stain (Invitrogen Molecular Probes, Carlsbad, CA, USA) binds to dsDNA and fluoresces blue, showing the nucleus (white arrow) of the cells of the mucosal layer in the gallbladder (green arrow) that have been stained green with phalloidin. Phalloidin binds to F-actin and is used to identify tissue structure and locations of actin reassortment (green regions) triggered by the infection. The S Typhi (red arrow) can be seen in red (O antigen stain) in a discrete cluster on the outside of the mucosal layer. Although not the only member of the Enterobacteriaceae bearing the O9 antigen, culture isolation of S Typhi from our patient's bile is strongly suggestive that these microorganisms are also S Typhi.Our patient did not have a documented history of enteric fever. In endemic areas such as Nepal, most people who undergo cholecystectomy for cholecystitis do not give an obvious, recent history of enteric fever, but gallbladder carriage of S Typhi and Paratyphi organisms is a well recognised means of spread. At last follow-up in December, 2013, the patient was doing well.
options: Typhus fever, Leishmaniasis, Echinococcosis, Typhoid fever

input: A healthy businessman aged in his 50s presented to our outpatient clinic at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, India, in March 2016 with sudden eruption of multiple swellings on the scalp of 3 months' duration. The condition had been treated empirically as deep folliculitis for the past 3 months by different care providers without any improvement. Six well-defined, firm, erythematous tumours with visible telangiectasiae along with several papulonodules were noted on the fronto-parietal scalp (figure, A).

A 79-year-old woman was referred to our department with a sudden onset of dyspnoea. She had end-stage kidney disease secondary to IgA nephropathy and, 6 months earlier, had started peritoneal dialysis. The patient did not report a cough, fever, or chills.On examination, her blood pressure was 154/93 mm Hg, heart rate 58 beats per min, oxygen saturation 91% room air, temperature 36·8°C. She had no oedema, nor any symptoms of right-sided heart failure. She had no abdominal pain. On chest auscultation, we found no breath sounds on the right side. Her weight had been stable.
A chest x-ray showed a new large right pleural effusion—a previous x-ray, done 11 months earlier, had been reported as clear.
Analysis of a sample of pleural fluid showed a clear yellow liquid with a cell count of 113 cells per mm3, composed of 2% neutrophils and 45% lymphocytes. The protein concentration of the pleural fluid was 5 g/L, glucose concentration was 7·9 mmol/L, and creatinine concentration was 498 μmol/L, indicating a likely transudate.
Blood tests showed a white blood count of 8·67 × 109 per L (normal 4·5–11·0), a C-reactive protein concentration of 0·8 mg/L (normal <5), glucose concentration of 5·4 mmol/L (normal 4·1–6·0), plasma protein concentration of 69 g/L (normal 66–87), albumin concentration of 32 g/L (normal 36–44), and a creatinine concentration of 512 μmol/L (normal range 45–84). Electrolytes and liver function tests were unremarkable.
The peritoneal dialysis fluid was clear and showed a glucose concentration of 7·8 g/L and creatinine of 484 μmol/L.
Peritoneal scintigraphy, combined with a single-photon-emission CT and CT (SPECT/CT) scan, showed radioactive tracer in the pleural cavity after infusion into the peritoneal cavity, confirming pleuro-peritoneal communication (figure, video). The patient's symptoms completely resolved on cessation of peritoneal dialysis. The recurrence of a pleural effusion, immediately on recommencing peritoneal dialysis, led us to decide on a definitive transfer to haemodialysis. After 8 months of follow-up, she remains asymptomatic, without any recurrence of a pleural effusion.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication is an uncommon complication of peritoneal dialysis, occurring in 1–2% of patients. The communication usually appears less than 3 months after initiating dialysis, but may also occur months to years later.
In 88% of cases, the pleural effusion is on the right side of the chest; left-sided defects are often covered by the heart and pericardium, making leakage on the left side less likely.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication takes place via congenital or acquired diaphragmatic defects and occurs when intra-abdominal pressure is increased by the administration of the peritoneal dialysis fluid.
A rapidly developed transudative unilateral pleural efffusion, with a high glucose concentration—dextrose being the most commonly used osmotic agent in peritoneal dialysis—accompanied by a high creatinine level, close to the dialysate composition, is highly suggestive of a leak of dialysate into the pleural cavity.
Dynamic imaging, such as SPECT/CT, shows the transfer of the radioactive tracer from the peritoneal to the pleural cavity and facilitates location of the site of the leak. Conservative treatment—temporary interruption of the peritoneal dialysis for 2–6 weeks—is effective in half of cases. Chemical pleurodesis or surgical interventions should be considered as second-line treatments, and the pros and cons of an invasive treatment should be weighed up against a definitive transfer to haemodialysis.
options: Congestive heart failure, Pleuro-peritoneal communication, Nephrotic syndrome, Malignant pleural effusion

input: A 76-year-old woman was referred to University Medical Center Utrecht (Utrecht, Netherlands) in August, 2016, for surgical resection of a tumour of the appendix (figure, A). CT scan showed homogeneous enhancing mass at the tip of the appendix, and because of the location and arterial enhancement, the lesion was thought to be a neuroendocrine tumour. To rule out metastases before surgery, a 68Ga-HA-DOTATATE PET–CT scan was done, showing intense tracer accumulation in the suspected lesion (maximum standardised uptake value of 29·8; figure, B) without any signs of metastases. After laparoscopic surgical resection, histopathological examination showed a sharply demarcated tumour composed of spindle cells with elongated nuclei without overt atypia and low mitotic and proliferative activity (Ki-67-positive cells <2%; figure, C). DNA sequencing showed a mutation in exon 11 of KIT proto-oncogene receptor tyrosine kinase (KIT; Gln575_Leu576delinsHis) and the tumour was strongly positive for c-KIT and anoctamin-1 consistent with criteria for gastrointestinal stromal tumour. Because of the positive PET scan, somatostatin receptor type 2 (SSTR2A) immunohistochemistry was done, which showed strong positivity for SSTR2A in the tumour (figure, D). Surgery was completed without any complications and the patient recovered quickly. Follow-up imaging will be done in March, 2017, in accordance with our national guideline for low-risk gastrointestinal stromal tumour.High expression of somatostatin receptors can be found in up to 81·9% (receptor subtype one) and 87·6% (subtype two) of gastrointestinal stromal tumours, and is therefore a much more reliable marker than immunohistochemical evidence of neuroendocrine differentiation, which might be seen in about 15% of tumours. Several gastrointestinal stromal tumours have also shown high uptake in 111In-pentetreotide scintigraphy. However, to our knowledge, no case of gastrointestinal stromal tumour detected by 68Ga-HA-DOTATATE has been described before. In malignant or high-grade gastrointestinal stromal tumours, 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET–CT is useful for detection, therapy response monitoring, and prognostication, but has little value in gastrointestinal stromal tumours with a low proliferative index. Somatostatin receptor-targeted PET–CT might be a valuable extension of the diagnostic repertoire and could also be used to select patients with metastasis for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy when no further surgical or chemotherapeutic options are available.
target: Neuroendocrine tumour, gastrointestinal stromal tumour, neuroblastoma
options: Neuroendocrine tumour, papillary thyroid carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, Gastrointestinal stromal tumour, colorectal carcinoma, neuroblastoma, Glioblastoma, meningioma, mucosa associated lympoid tissue lymphoma, Neuroendocrine tumour, gastrointestinal stromal tumour, neuroblastoma

A 30-year-old man presented to our department in Leiden, Netherlands, with a 6-year history of recurrent solitary swellings. On average, he had 15 episodes per year. The swellings had started on his abdomen and had gradually moved to his chest, neck, and, more recently, his face. The swellings varied in size, were painless, appeared spontaneously, and resolved after 5–7 days. Treatment with high-dose antihistamine had had no effect. There were no other symptoms. The patient was otherwise healthy and did not take any medication.Physical examination revealed a swelling of the right cheek and upper lip. Photos of previous episodes revealed similar swellings of the left cheek (figure, A). The differential diagnoses included angio-oedema, granulomatous cheilitis, sialadenitis, sialolithiasis, and Kimura's disease, but these could not be confirmed by laboratory examination, histopathology, or clinical examination by a dental surgeon. Laboratory examinations, including eosinophil count and C1 esterase inhibitor concentrations, were completely normal except for IgE concentrations, which were elevated (3736 IU/mL, normal range is 0–99). A biopsy of the buccal mucosa showed a dense eosinophilic infiltrate. Ultrasound examination and MRI scan revealed a non-specific infiltration and enhancement of the subcutis.
The elevated IgE concentration and eosinophil in-filtration in the biopsy suggested a parasitic infection. A further inquiry revealed that the patient had consumed raw fish in Taiwan before the first swelling episode. Western blot analysis of serum for reactivity against crude antigens of Gnathostoma spinigerum third-stage larvae (L3) showed the presence of a specific 24 kDa band that was diagnostic for gnathostomiasis. Gnathostomiasis is a helminthic zoonosis, endemic in southeast Asia, which is transmitted through ingestion of larvae of G spinigerum in raw or undercooked fresh water fish, eels, frogs, reptiles, or birds. After ingestion, larvae penetrate the gastrointestinal wall and migrate through the subcutaneous tissue, causing typical migratory swellings and eosinophilia that can recur for years.
A revision of the MRI scan identified a larva of approximately 4·0×0·2 cm (figure, B). The patient was treated with ivermectin 0·2 mg/kg once per day on 2 consecutive days. This treatment was successful because it stimulated the outward migration of the larva (an impression of the head of the larva became visible in the lower lip; appendix), which caused a temporary increase of the swelling. Eosinophilia was now present (1·03×109 cells per L, normal value is <0·50 × 109 cells per L). Further treatment, aiming to preclude potential migration towards the eye socket, consisted of albendazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days. The symptoms resolved within a few days and the patient remains symptom free.
options: Angio-oedema, Granulomatous cheilitis, Gnathostomiasis, Kimura's disease

input: In June, 2014, a 37-year-old man with known end-stage renal disease and chronic uraemic pericardial effusion presented to our institution with gradually worsening dyspnoea and orthopnoea, 4 days after a nephrectomy to control hypertension. He had been having regular haemodialysis three-times per week for the preceding 9 years after rejection of a transplanted kidney. On examination he was severely dyspnoeic at rest, and had a pulse rate of 102 beats per min, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, and blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg with 25 mm Hg paradoxical changes. Lung auscultation showed left basilar bronchial breath sounds. Chest radiography indicated cardiomegaly with an air–fluid level at the level of the heart (figure). Chest CT showed hydropneumopericardium (figure). Echocardiography showed a massive pericardial effusion causing more than 25% respiratory variation of mitral inflow, consistent with tamponade physiology. We made a pericardial window and drained about 1 L of serosangiunous fluid. Pericardial fluid culture was negative and pericardial biopsy analysis showed acute and chronic inflammation and fibrosis. The patient had an uneventful hospital course after therapeutic drainage. 2 weeks later, follow-up echocardiography showed only mild pericardial effusion. In December, 2014, the patient was well, with echocardiography showing only mild pericardial effusion. In March, 2015, the patient was in a generally good condition but remained on the haemodialysis ward at the Namazi teaching hospital.Pneumopericardium usually happens after blunt or penetrating chest trauma, but is occasionally seen after intubation and mechanical ventilation. Except for recent intubation for nephrectomy, we could not find any risk factors in our patient. Rarely, pneumopericardium can superimpose on pre-existing pericardial effusion and lead to tension hydropneumopericardium, as in our patient. The plain radiographic imaging can resemble a large hiatal hernia or gastric torsion; a delineated heart border within an air–fluid level is helpful to exclude these differential diagnoses.
options: Gastric torsion, Achalasia, Pneumopericardium, Hiatal hernia

A 37-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of recurrent episodes of flushing of the right side of her face after exercise and hot baths (figure). She explained that the flushing resolved after each episode following 1 h of rest. She reported no medical history.On examination, we found no abnormalities: specifically, the patient's nervous system—including her cranial nerves—was intact. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable—including full blood count, liver and kidney function tests, electrolyte concentrations, thyroid function tests, tumour markers, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein concentration. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest, a carotid artery ultrasound, and enhanced MRIs of her head, neck, and cervical and thoracic spine, and cervicobrachial plexus were normal.
Considering the patient's symptoms and the absence of any pathology that might explain her presentation, we made a diagnosis of harlequin syndrome.
After an explanation of the diagnosis and reassurance of the patient, we decided not to offer her any treatment since she was not particularly troubled by the symptoms. At follow-up she reported that the flushing continued and that she was otherwise well.
Harlequin syndrome is characterised by unilateral facial flushing and sweating induced by exercise, heat, and emotion; most cases are idiopathic. However, a thorough examination and an extensive investigation are mandatory in order to rule out all known causes—including a brainstem infarction, multiple sclerosis, syringomyelia, thyroid diseases, a superior mediastinum neurinoma, schwannoma at the lung apex, Pancoast tumour, and dissection of the internal carotid artery.
Unilateral disturbance of the sympathetic innervation of the face leading to an inability of the facial vasculature to dilate in response to normal stimuli is thought to be the cause of harlequin syndrome: a unilateral lack of flushing and sweating.
It should not be confused with Horner's syndrome—a unilateral ptosis, reactive ipsilateral miosis, and hemifacial anhidrosis—although they share similar lesion sites and some clinical manifestations. Most patients with harlequin syndrome—as in our case—do not require medical or surgical treatment unless, of course, there is an underlying disease (video).
options: Dissection of the carotid artery, Upper mediastinal neoplasia, Pituitary tumour, Toxic goitre

A 58-year-old man was hospitalised in our intensive care unit for severe, acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by an influenza virus infection. After 31 days, he was gradually weaned off mechanical ventilation. However, on the day after extubation, he had to be reintubated because of further respiratory distress. Emergency intubation was performed after rapid sequence induction using the short-acting anaesthetic agent etomidate, intravenously, at a dose of 0·3 mg/kg, and the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, intravenously, at a dose of 1 mg/kg. Orotracheal intubation was done without any difficulty. However, immediately after intubation, a change was noted on the electrocardiogram (ECG) (figure) and the patient became pulseless. The ECG showed ventricular tachycardia, which developed into ventricular fibrillation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated along with medical treatments to reduce his serum potassium concentration, which was 9·6 mmol/L; 1 h after the cardiac arrest, the serum potassium returned to within the normal range at 3·3 mmol/L. Of note, our patient had no contraindications to the use of succinylcholine before the reintubation—specifically, his serum potassium concentration was 3·5 mmol/L and he had no neurological signs or muscle weakness.Closer examination of the ECG clearly showed the effects of hyperkalaemia on the heart during the incident: initially, the PR interval was prolonged and the T waves were tented (figure), next the P waves were lost, ST segment changes were seen, and the QRS complexes were prolonged (figure), and finally the QRS complex widened in a sine-wave configuration (figure). Succinylcholine is the first line neuromuscular blocking agent for rapid sequence induction because it is fast-acting. It causes depolarisation of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) located in the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) leading to the efflux of intracellular potassium into the plasma. In cases of muscle denervation, including patients who have been in intensive care for a prolonged period, AChRs are upregulated in both the NMJ and throughout the muscle membrane; immature forms of AChRs are also released. These immature receptors are more sensitive to agonists with depolarisation occurring at lower concentrations and lasting for a longer time with no desensitisation. Succinylcholine in such situations can lead to a massive efflux of potassium from muscles to the plasma, with life-threatening consequences.
In cases of severe hyperkalaemia, treatment should include intravenous calcium salt—chloride or gluconate—to raise the threshold potential and to stabilise the myocardium, and drugs that promote cellular potassium reuptake—eg, insulin, sodium bicarbonate, and β2 agonists. This case serves as a reminder that succinylcholine should be used with caution in patients who have been in the intensive care unit for a prolonged period even without so-called intensive care unit acquired weakness.
options: Acute coronary syndrome, Succinylcholine induced hyperkalaemia, Anaphylactic reaction, Malignant hyperthermia

A 33-year-old homeless woman presented to the emergency room in September, 2012, with 2 days of dry cough, dyspnoea, and fever, and 1 week of pruritic rash. On examination she had a temperature of 41·0°C, blood pressure of 98/65 mm Hg, heart rate of 85 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 bpm, and O2 saturation of 47% on room air. She had a diffuse papular rash with vesicles of different ages with haemorrhagic crust affecting the trunk, extremities, face, and scalp, but sparing the palms and soles (figure). She had normal mental status, cranial nerves, motor, and sensory examination. Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral airspace opacities.
Within a few hours of presentation she suddenly became confused, with flaccid paralysis necessitating intubation and admission to the medical intensive care unit. Electroencephalogram showed non-convulsive status epilepticus. MRI brain showed multiple foci of punctate microhaemorrhages throughout the corpus callosum, both temporal lobes, and left posterior cingulate gyrus, consistent with infectious haemorrhagic encephalitis (figure). HIV testing was positive, with CD4 count 4 cells/μL (normal 348–1456 cells/μL), and viral load was 66 000 copies/mL (normal < 50 copies/mL). A skin biopsy sample stained positive for varicella zoster virus (VZV), but negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV).
Zoster-associated encephalitis from disseminated VZV can develop within days of the disseminated rash, and should be strongly suspected in immunosuppressed patients. Characteristic signs of zoster-associated encephalitis include acute delirium, typical signs of stroke such as headache with acute hemiplegia, aphasia, ataxia, hemisensory loss, or visual changes, dependent on the predominant location of the VZV vasculitis. Intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h for 7–10 days should be started early if there is clinical suspicion of encephalitis.
Our patient was given intravenous aciclovir and multiple antiepileptic drugs to control her seizures. We treated her for VZV pneumonia, aspergillus pneumonia, propofol-induced pancreatitis, Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, and critical illness myopathy. After stabilisation in hospital she was started on antiretrovirals and pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis. After 2 months of rehabilitation she could walk independently and communicate without difficulty. At last follow-up in March, 2014, she had made a near full recovery in terms of her cognitive and motor function.
options: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Chickenpox, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, Disseminated varicella zoster virus infection
