A 58-year-old man with a 31-month history of seeing peoples’ faces as distorted and, in his words, appearing “demonic” visited our laboratory for assessment. The patient stated that the distortions—severely stretched features of the face, with deep grooves on the forehead, cheeks, and chin—were present on every person's face he encountered, but he reported no distortions when looking at objects, such as houses or cars. The patient said that even though faces were distorted, he was still able to recognise who they were. Notably, he reported no distortions when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper. The distortions were not accompanied by delusional beliefs about the identities of the people he encountered—such as his family or friends.
The patient had a history of bipolar affective disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Additionally, he had a significant head injury at the age of 43 years that led to hospitalisation. He also had possible carbon monoxide poisoning at the age of 55 years, which occurred 4 months prior to the onset of his distortion symptoms. He was not prescribed any medications. He reported no use of illicit substances.
On initial assessment, the patient was well and not distressed; he had some mild low back discomfort. The distortions were very distressing to him initially, he said, but he had become habituated to them. Neuropsychological testing indicated no obvious abnormal general cognitive function; Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. He had no deficits of visual acuity (10/10 in both eyes) or colour vision (Ishira plates: 25/25; Farnsworth–Munsell 100-hue test: average discrimination). Computer-based face perception tests indicated mild impairment in recognition of facial identity but normal recognition of facial expression. No laboratory investigations were done at this stage.
Whole-brain T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI scans showed a round lesion—T1 dark and T2 bright—measuring approximately 1 cm, located on the superior aspect of the head of the left hippocampus, displacing it inferiorly about 3 mm; despite this, the internal anatomy of the left hippocampus was preserved. The impression from the neurologist was that the lesion was probably an arachnoid cyst in the left hippocampal head; other observations included normal ventricle size, unremarkable midline structures, clear paranasal sinuses, and mild cerebral atrophy.
At 1-year follow-up, a repeated MRI showed no change in the size of the cyst.
As the patient reported no distortion when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper, we asked him to compare an in-person face to a photograph of the face taken in the same room under identical lighting conditions. By alternating between observing the in-person face—perceived as distorted—and the photo on a computer screen—perceived as undistorted—he provided real-time feedback on the perceived differences. We then used image-editing software to modify each photo until it matched his in-person perception (figure).Based on the patient's description of his visual perception, the neuropsychological assessment, and the distortion visualisations, we concluded that he had prosopometamorphopsia.
Prosopometamorphopsia is a rare neurological disorder of visual perception in which faces appear distorted in shape, texture, position, or colour. In most cases, the distortions occur all the time, whether the patient sees the face in person, on a screen, or on paper, thus making it difficult for patients to assess the accuracy of illustrations depicting their perceptual abnormalities because the illustration itself will appear distorted.
Prosopometamorphopsia's aetiology is varied and can occur in the context of head trauma, cerebral infarction, epilepsy, migraine, and hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder. The disorder can also manifest without detectable structural brain changes.
Our patient's unusual phenomenology, combined with computer software, enabled us to generate photorealistic visualisations of the distortions he experienced. Such images, we believe, have not been generated before (video).
options: Prosopagnosia, Prosopometamorphopsia, Capgras syndrome, Palinopsia

A 30-year-old white man with no ocular history presented to eye casualty in Sidcup in October, 2012, with bilateral central visual loss, following inhalation of poppers. On examination his visual acuity was 6/12 on the right and 6/18 in the left eye. Slit lamp biomicroscopy showed subtle macular changes in the form of yellow foveal spots (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography showed clear disruption of the foveal cone inner segment–outer segment layer (figure). At follow-up 6 months later, the patient's visual acuity and examination findings remained unchanged, despite cessation of poppers use.
Poppers (slang for various alkyl nitrite compounds) are commonly used in the gay community, for their ability to relax the anal sphincter and known psychoactive effects. Following changes to legislation in 2006, poppers' main ingredient, isobutyl nitrite, was substituted for isopropyl nitrite. Since then, there have been several reports of a new form of visual loss termed poppers maculopathy. The exact mechanism by which poppers cause damage to central photoreceptors is unknown, but there is a clear cause–effect relationship. Despite online warnings outlining the risks of poppers, the number of individuals presenting with associated visual loss is increasing. Fundoscopy findings can be very subtle, with more striking changes seen on optical coherence tomography. The relatively easy availability and widespread use of poppers is underestimated and concerning, given the propensity for permanent damage to the eyes. We would encourage both end-users and healthcare professionals to be aware of the potentially serious and irreversible damage poppers can have on vision.
options: Solar retinopathy, Poppers maculopathy, Central serous chorioretinopathy, Adult vitelliform macular dystrophy

A 34-year-old man, from sub-Saharan Africa, was referred to our hospital for short stature, when he came to France, as an actor, to play the part of a child. The patient reported that at birth he required incubator support and that his growth was blunted from early childhood.At our first evaluation, his height was 137 cm, weight was 26·4 kg, and body-mass index 14 kg/m2. He had long extremities compared to his trunk and he had signs of hypogonadism—including small intrascrotal testes (0·5 mL; typical 12–30 in adult males), absent pubic and axillary hair, micro-penis (2 cm), and a high-pitched voice.
Hormone assays showed combined pituitary hormone deficiencies with low serum morning cortisol and undetectable dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphate with low adrenocorticotropin; low thyroxine and triiodothyronine; undetectable testosterone and oestradiol; low inhibin B and low gonadotrophins; low prolactin; and growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 were both below detectable limits (appendix).
Brain MRI showed marked pituitary gland hypoplasia, absence of pituitary stalk and ectopic posterior hypophysis, and no extra-pituitary abnormalities.
The patient's bone age was 13 years, and knee MRI showed persistent growth plates at the distal femoral or proximal tibial epiphysis. Genetic testing did not identify pathogenic variants in any of the genes responsible for congenital hypopituitarism.
We commenced treatment with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and recombinant human growth hormone replacement for 2 months before the patient had to return to his country as his visa had expired; he was provided with growth hormone cartridges for an additional 3 months.
Figure Congenital hypopituitarism treated in adulthood
Show full caption
Figure viewer
The patient returned to France 3 years later; his height was 142 cm, but otherwise, his clinical state was unchanged. We commenced stepwise replacement with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, growth hormone, and gonadotropins for the next 4 years. His height increased to 161 cm—an increase of 24 cm—and he achieved normal pubertal development (appendix). During the increase in height, the patient developed scoliosis which necessitated surgical correction and an arthrodesis at T2-L1 (appendix).
At baseline, cardiac MRI showed a small heart—but well-proportioned to the patient's body size—with normal contractile function; hormone treatment resulted in linear, uniform growth of the heart with a progressive increase in ventricular mass and volume. Concomitant decrease in the extracellular space indicated that the cardiac growth resulted from cardiomyocyte correction of hypotrophy; the initial rapid decrease in extracellular space, after levothyroxine and hydrocortisone were started, was mostly attributed to resorption of myxoedematous infiltration, and possibly due to inflammation.
Growth hormone—given prior to puberty induction—transiently increased ventricular contractility to supraphysiologic values, with the ejection fraction reaching 78%; it normalised during gonadotrophin therapy. Left ventricular stroke volume increased proportionally compared to end-diastolic volume, reflecting the heart's ability to enhance its contractile strength in response to increased venous return—Frank-Starling law.
We further observed a uniform increase of the cross-sectional area of the patient's femoral muscles during treatment accompanied by a progressive decrease of intramuscular fat fraction. Growth hormone induced transient glucose intolerance, which resolved during further therapy.
Congenital hypopituitarism is usually diagnosed and treated during childhood or adolescence to correct blunted growth and lack of pubertal development. Rarely is hormone replacement initiated in adulthood, and results of such cases are limited. Regarding the heart, the capacity to generate cardiomyocytes during adult life has been the subject of much debate; cardiomyogenesis is minimal in healthy humans after birth. Metachronous heart growth—as seen in our patient—from size of a child to a normal adult, has not previously been reported. In conclusion, hormone replacement, administered gradually, in an adult patient with congenital hypopituitarism can safely induce heart growth normalisation proportionate to linear growth (video).
options: Cortisol, testosterone, and thyroxine, Dehydroepiandrosterone, testosterone, and oestradiol, Corticotropin, cortisol, and testosterone, Dehydroepiandrosterone, testosterone, and inhibin B

A 27-year-old man presented to an emergency department with vomiting and an altered mental state. He had a history of possible Gilbert's syndrome as a child and previous opiate use disorder, but with no evidence of recent use. He gave a family history of a maternal grandfather who had developed seizures during a hospital admission for asthma. The patient had otherwise been fit and well and physically active—including playing hockey. While in the emergency department he became combative and left the hospital against medical advice.Laboratory investigations taken just before he left showed a raised blood ammonia concentration of 155 μmol/L (normal 16–60).
4 days before attending the hospital, he had epidural injections of the corticosteroid triamcinolone at two spinal levels because of chronic back pain. Soon after the procedure, the patient reported a headache and feeling unwell.
The day after his presentation to an emergency department, the patient's father called 911 saying that the patient was behaving strangely and having violent outbursts; he also said that the day before, he and his son had an episode of vomiting after eating a takeaway meal.
When the patient attended the emergency department for the second time, he immediately had a seizure. He was intubated and transferred to our university hospital. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
On examination, the patient had bilateral, fixed, dilated pupils, and he made minimal response to physical stimulation.
Investigations showed that the ammonia concentration had increased further to 591 μmol/L; serum creatinine kinase concentration was 299 units per L (normal 20–200), aspartate aminotransferase 26 units per L (normal <40), alanine aminotransferase 65 units per L (normal <41), alkaline phosphatase 84 units per L (normal 40–129), and total bilirubin concentration was 3 mg/dL (normal <1·2), and screening for paracetamol, salicylates, valproic acid, and serum ethanol was negative.
A CT scan of the patient's head showed diffuse cerebral oedema with effacement of both lateral ventricles (figure).
Despite treatment, including intravenous 3% hypertonic saline, levocarnitine, lactulose, and mannitol, the patient's condition continued to deteriorate, and 3 days after he arrived at our hospital, he was pronounced brain dead.
Further investigations into the cause of death—including genetic testing for urea cycle disorders—showed a mutation indicative of X-linked ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency. The patient's family members have been advised to have genetic screening.
The commonest cause of hyperammonaemia in adults is liver disease—specifically cirrhosis. However, congenital disorders—such as urea cycle defects—should also be considered, even later in life.
OTC deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder and it can present at any age; late-onset disease is usually seen in heterozygous females. Adult-onset presentations can be triggered by infection, stress, fasting, surgery, increased protein intake, and medications—including glucocorticoids. Our case emphasises the need for timely recognition of unexplained life-threatening hyperammonaemia and the prompt employment of treatment with ammonia scavengers, arginine and citrulline supplements, and haemodialysis. Liver transplantation is also an option in the management of patients with severe urea cycle disorders.

A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. He was admitted to the paediatric nephrology unit for evaluation following a generalised seizure, persistent stage 2 hypertension, and melaena for one week requiring packed red cell transfusion. Significant examination findings included severe thinness (BMI-for-age –5·2 standard deviation score), stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 136/110 mm Hg), pallor, and generalised muscle tenderness. Investigations identified normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 85 g/L), acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 353·6 μmol/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (serum ferritin 3312 pmol/L, serum C-reactive protein 146 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h). Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4–5 red blood cells per high power field).
On diagnostic evaluation, serum antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative and C3 and C4 complement protein concentrations were normal. Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac–mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. Considering the characteristic angiographic findings, multisystem presentation (fever, myalgia, hypertension, and central nervous system, gastrointestinal, and renal involvement) and laboratory features of inflammation, the patient was diagnosed with childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa. Clinical exome sequencing excluded inherited deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2 mutation).
Therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (30 mg/kg per day for 3 days) was followed by oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg per day for 4 weeks, gradually tapered to 5 mg/day over the next 16 weeks. The day after finishing the three methylprednisolone pulses, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses (500 mg/m2 per dose) were started once a month for 6 months. Vasculitis-induced ischemia resulted in generalised myalgia, anuric acute kidney injury requiring maintenance haemodialysis, stage 2 hypertension that was controlled on concomitant therapy with five oral antihypertensive medications (amlodipine, 0·6 mg/kg per day; prazocin, 0·6 mg/kg per day; enalapril, 0·6 mg/kg per day; metoprolol, 3·0 mg/kg per day; and clonidine, 5·0 mcg/kg per day), and nervous system involvement with seizures requiring two oral antiseizure medications (initially phenytoin, 5·0 mg/kg per day; which was changed to levetiracetam, 20·0 mg/kg per day). During treatment initiation with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and the first cyclophosphamide pulse, mesenteric ischaemia deteriorated into gut perforation, requiring bowel resection and re-anastomosis. Post-operative peritonitis and septicaemia required intravenous broad-spectrum antimicrobials (renal-modified doses; piperacillin–tazobactam, 210 mg/kg per day; teicoplanin, 5 mg/kg per day; metronidazole, 30 mg/kg per day; and caspofungin, 50 mg/m2 per day) and intravenous vasopressors (adrenaline and noradrenaline, titrated to 1 μg/kg per min). The overall disease was severe, reflected by a Factor-Five Score of 3. Discharged under multidisciplinary follow-up, the patient was receiving oral prednisolone (0·5 mg/kg per day, on tapering), oral mycophenolate mofetil (500 mg/m2 per day), and maintenance haemodialysis (done locally) at the last teleconsultation.
Childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa is a rare, severe condition that requires prompt recognition and management. Patients with Factor-Five Scores exceeding 2 have a fulminant course of polyarteritis nodosa with a high risk of mortality and long-term morbidities. This case illustrates the role of early diagnosis and treatment in preventing mortality and improving outcomes.

#### 1. Diagnostic Criteria and Gold Standard Tests for Leptospirosis
- **Knowledge Content**: Leptospirosis is diagnosed using a combination of clinical criteria, exposure history, and laboratory tests. Clinical criteria often include acute fever, headache, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and evidence of renal or hepatic involvement. The gold standard test is the Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT), which detects antibodies against Leptospira species and requires paired sera (acute and convalescent) for confirmation. Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) testing for Leptospira DNA in blood or urine is highly specific and useful early in the disease. Other supportive tests include ELISA for IgM antibodies and culture (though culture is slow and less practical).
- **How it Helps**: In this case, the patient's symptoms (fever, vomiting, diarrhea), physical exam findings (likely conjunctival suffusion and jaundice), lab results (AKI, elevated aminotransferases, bilirubin), and exposure history (fall into a canal) align perfectly with clinical criteria for leptospirosis. Ordering MAT or PCR would confirm the diagnosis, but the clinical presentation is already highly suggestive.

#### 2. Differential Diagnosis for Acute Fever with Hepatorenal Syndrome
- **Knowledge Content**: Acute fever with hepatorenal syndrome (concurrent liver and kidney injury) can be caused by several conditions:
  - **Viral Hepatitis (e.g., Hepatitis A or E)**: Causes fever, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes, but acute kidney injury is less common and typically not as prominent without other factors.
  - **Sepsis or Septic Shock**: Can lead to multi-organ failure, including AKI and liver dysfunction, but often has a focus of infection (e.g., pneumonia) and may not have the specific exposure history.
  - **Hantavirus Infection**: Presents with fever, renal failure, and sometimes liver involvement, but is often associated with respiratory symptoms and rodent exposure in endemic areas, not water exposure.
  - **Malaria**: In endemic regions, can cause fever, jaundice, and AKI, but typically has a travel history and cyclic fever patterns.
  - **Leptospirosis**: Distinctly associated with water exposure, conjunctival suffusion, and a biphasic illness course, making it a top differential.
- **How it Helps**: This differential analysis shows that leptospirosis is the best fit due to the water exposure history and the combination of symptoms. Other conditions like viral hepatitis or sepsis lack the specific epidemiological clue (canal fall) or typical physical findings (e.g., conjunctival suffusion).

#### 3. Typical Incubation Period and Clinical Course of Leptospirosis
- **Knowledge Content**: The incubation period for leptospirosis ranges from 2 to 30 days, with a median of 5-14 days. The clinical course is often biphasic: an acute septicemic phase (days 1-7) with fever, chills, headache, myalgia, and gastrointestinal symptoms; followed by an immune phase (days 7-30) where complications like Weil's disease (icteric form with jaundice, AKI, hemorrhage) or meningitis may occur. Symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea are common in the acute phase.
- **How it Helps**: The patient's exposure (fall into a canal) three weeks prior aligns with the incubation period (21 days is within the 2-30 day range). The current symptoms (2-day history of fever, vomiting, diarrhea) suggest the acute phase or early immune phase, with lab findings indicating progression to Weil's disease. This timeline strongly supports leptospirosis.

#### 4. Comparison with Other Waterborne Diseases That Cause Similar Symptoms
- **Knowledge Content**: Waterborne diseases that might present with fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, or systemic involvement include:
  - **Giardiasis**: Causes diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and bloating, but fever is uncommon, and it does not typically involve AKI or liver injury.
  - **Cryptosporidiosis**: Leads to watery diarrhea and can cause fever in immunocompromised individuals, but hepatorenal syndrome is rare.
  - **Hepatitis A**: Transmitted via contaminated water, presents with fever, nausea, jaundice, and elevated liver enzymes, but AKI is not a hallmark.
  - **Cholera**: Characterized by profuse watery diarrhea and dehydration, but fever is absent or mild, and there is no liver or kidney involvement beyond dehydration effects.
  - **Leptospirosis**: Unique in its ability to cause a systemic illness with specific multi-organ damage (liver and kidney) following water exposure, often with conjunctival involvement.
- **How it Helps**: Among waterborne diseases, only leptospirosis consistently presents with the full spectrum of fever, gastrointestinal symptoms, hepatorenal syndrome, and a relevant exposure history. This comparison rules out options like giardiasis or hepatitis A, which do not explain all findings (e.g., AKI).

### Overall Diagnostic Implication
The retrieved knowledge confirms that leptospirosis is the most likely diagnosis. The exposure history, incubation period, clinical symptoms, physical exam clues (inferred from context), and laboratory evidence of hepatorenal syndrome are all classic for leptospirosis, particularly Weil's disease. A 37-year-old woman with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, and dyspnoea, attended our clinic for investigation.
12 months earlier, the patient had embolisation of pelvic varicose veins, using glue and lipiodised oil, for pelvic venous disorder; she had reported a history of pelvic congestion syndrome with chronic pelvic pain beginning after a pregnancy 5 years earlier. The pain worsened just before the onset of menstruation. She also had symptomatic varicose veins in her legs. Venograms had confirmed abdominal-pelvic venous insufficiency with reflux in a dilated left ovarian vein, tortuous pelvic varicosities near the uterus, and bilateral dilated utero-vaginal venous plexuses.
The patient had no history of recent viral infection or neck pain; she was prescribed no medication.
On examination the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 132/70 mm Hg, her pulse was 97 beats per min, and her BMI was 20·7 kg/m2. She had a firm, hard moderate-sized goitre but no signs of Graves’ orbitopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed hyperthyroidism; the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration was biologically undetectable, the free thyroxine (FT4) concentration was above 100·0 pmol/L (typical range 12·0–22·0), and the free triiodothyroxine (FT3) concentration was 36·0 pmol/L (typical range 3·1–6·8). Tests for TSH-receptor antibodies were negative. Thyroglobulin concentration was 1143 ng/mL (typical range 3·5–77·0); C-reactive protein concentration was within typical range (<5 mg/L). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies were also within the normal range. Urinary iodine concentration was raised at 10·01 μmol/L (typical range 0·35–1·60).
123Iodine thyroid scintigraphy showed no significant uptake with a blunted measured value of 0·4% at 120 min (average value 12% at 120 min for a mean TSH of 1·2 mIU/L in France; appendix).
Considering the findings in the round, we ruled out thyrotoxicosis factitia because of the raised thyroglobulin concentration and concluded the most likely diagnosis was an iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis. As stated above, the patient was not prescribed amiodarone—a recognised cause of iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis—or any other drugs associated with thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, and she had no history of recent radiographic contrast exposure. However, an unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed lipiodised oil in the ovarian veins (figure 1); additionally, an unenhanced CT scan of the patient's neck, which we requested to give further weight to our conclusion that the patient had thyrotoxicosis secondary to the lipiodised oil, showed a very high density of the thyroid (147 Hounsfield units [HU]; typical range 80–100; figure 2).
The patient was commenced on oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day until laboratory investigations showed she was euthyroid; the corticosteroids were gradually reduced over 5 months.
At follow-up 18 months later, she was well with normal thyroid function.
Excessive intake of iodine can cause hyperthyroidism; mainly this occurs after exposure to iodinated radiographic material or treatment with amiodarone. Interestingly, a study proposed a cutoff level of 117 HU for the density of the thyroid seen on unenhanced CT scan to distinguish patients with amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism from healthy controls and from euthyroid amiodarone-treated patients (appendix). With this in mind, we suggest that a hyperdense thyroid, seen on an unenhanced CT scan—with a density level above 120 HU—should raise the possibility of iodine overload and subsequent testing of the serum TSH concentration.
options: Subacute de Quervain thyroiditis, Graves’ disease, Iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis, Thyrotoxicosis factitia

A 41-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The patient gave no history of recent travel, previous abdominal surgery, or adverse reactions to any allergens. She had no past medical problems. However, 2 days before we saw her, the patient had a gastrointestinal endoscopy which found no abnormalities; gastroduodenal and colonic mucosal biopsies had also been reported as healthy.On examination we found the patient to be generally well; heart rate was 92 beats per min, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98%. She was afebrile. Her abdomen was tender and distended with bulging flanks and shifting dullness: indicative of ascites.
Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis (19·54 × 109 per L; normal 4·5–11·0) associated with a significant eosinophilia of 8·94 × 109 per L (normal 0–0·5), a raised IgE concentration (208 IU/mL; normal 1·5–144), and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein concentration (43 mg/L; normal <3·1). CA125 concentration was elevated (83 units/mL; normal 0–35); no other tumour marker was positive. Serum tryptase concentration was normal and tests screening for autoimmune diseases—including antinuclear antibodies for systemic lupus erythematosus or scleroderma—found nothing abnormal.
A CT scan excluded any visceral lesions. A diagnostic paracentesis showed eosinophilic ascites (figure). Blood, stool, and ascites analyses, including specific serological examinations and cultures, excluded viral, bacterial, and parasitic infections. That some parasitic infections, such as Strongyloides stercoralis, can be hard to diagnose based on one stool sample, led us to do repeated parasitological examinations of different stool samples, which all showed no positive results.
Lymphocytic and myeloproliferative forms of hypereosinophilic syndrome were excluded: a bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities. Using RT-PCR, no FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene was found, and T-cell-receptor gene rearrangement testing of the patient's peripheral blood was negative. A QuantiFERON-TB test was also negative.
We suspected a case of eosinophilic gastroenteritis, but to rule out any intra-abdominal neoplasm and to collect biopsies from the caecum serosa, we did a laparoscopy. Histopathological analysis of biopsy specimens confirmed our suspicions: significant eosinophilic infiltration with greater than 20 eosinophiles per high-power field; the small vessels were not involved, ruling out an associated vasculitis (figure). The patient was started on oral methylprednisolone and her symptoms rapidly improved; the serum eosinophilia returned to a typical level.
Three patterns of eosinophilic gastroenteritis are described: mucosal, mural, and serosal. Diagnosis of the serosal form is often considered a challenge as clinical and radiological presentations can be atypical. Likewise, histological findings can be misleading, as mucosal biopsies in the serosal form of eosinophilic gastroenteritis may appear normal, unlike those of the serosal layers which can confirm the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is usually made based on the combined biological, radiological, and histological findings. Finally, a good response to oral corticosteroids—as happened in our patient—adds weight to making a correct diagnosis of eosinophilic gastroenteritis.

input: A 14-year-old boy with early-onset guttate psoriasis vulgaris presented at our clinic with several reddish-purple, horizontal streaks on the distal part of his shins. Previously, he had been treated with narrow-band ultraviolet B, topical corticosteroids ranging from mild (hydrocortisone 17-butyrate cream 1 mg/g) to moderate (mometasone furoate cream 1 mg/g and betamethasone valerate ointment 1 mg/g), and tacrolimus ointment 1 mg/g—but the response to treatment was not long lasting. The family consulted a licensed practitioner of traditional Chinese medicine who prescribed a so-called herbal cream (figure). The patient applied the cream topically on the psoriatic lesions twice a day. After 9 months of doing this, he developed a new rash on his shins that was later confirmed to be striae distensae (figure). We suspected that the cause was exposure to a corticosteroid—but the patient had not been using a corticosteroid either topically or systemically during this time. The so-called herbal cream was suspected as a possible source; however, the content label only listed herbal ingredients including Chinese sumac, Sophora flavescens, Stemona tuberosa Lour. Nevertheless, the location of the striae was very unusual, and as a simple test, the herbal cream was applied on the upper arm of the senior physician; after 12 h, a strong vasoconstriction effect was seen (figure), which further raised our suspicion that the cream contained a corticosteroid. We therefore sent it for analysis at the Department of Official Medicines Control Laboratory, Swedish Medical Products Agency, Uppsala, Sweden. The laboratory used liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry and nuclear magnetic resonance, and reported that the cream contained both a potent corticosteroid (0·065% clobetasol propionate) and the antifungals ketoconazole and miconazole. We then reported this herbal product to the Danish Medicines Agency to ensure that it was dealt with appropriately.Prolonged exposure to traditional herbal creams or ointments resulting in cutaneous striae has previously been reported, and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has warned about a so-called natural Chinese herbal remedy—Yiganerjing Cream—containing the same ingredients as in our case. Furthermore, the hazards and adverse effects of herbal products are not confined to dermatology. The under-regulation of medicinal products is widespread, and the consequences of patients using such substances can be seen in clinics from all specialities. Patients who fail to respond adequately to conventional treatments often seek alternative treatment and as a result might expose themselves to potentially harmful agents. The importance of being vigilant when seeing patients taking and using herbal creams and remedies remains key to reaching the correct diagnosis. With such substances being freely available over the internet, the problem is likely to worsen.
options: Cutaneous striae, Lichen sclerosus, Scars, Linear focal elastosis

A 57-year-old woman without underlying disease was referred by her family doctor to Kaohsiung Municipal Ta-Tung Hospital (Kaohsiung, Taiwan) in October, 2017, for presenting with abdominal fullness lasting for several months. A huge heteroechoic hepatic mass was identified by abdominal ultrasound. Laboratory data revealed mildly elevated liver enzymes (glutamate-oxaloacetate transaminase 44 IU/L and glutamate-pyruvate transaminase 61 IU/L) and elevated total bilirubin (1·9 mg/dL). CT scan revealed a 20-cm tumour in the right hepatic lobe, enhanced in the arterial phase and washed out in the portal and delayed phases (figure, A).The pathological analysis of tissue sample collected by echo-guided aspiration showed cell necrosis, suggesting possible hepatocellular carcinoma with central necrosis, an inoperable disease. However, the tumour markers showed normal levels of α-fetoprotein (1·32 ng/ml). This finding led us to re-review the abdominal CT scan. We discovered a tiny so-called fat plane between the tumour and the liver (figure, B), causing us to re-diagnose the lesion as a retroperitoneal tumor. Because adrenal tumors are a potential differential diagnosis of retroperitoneal tumours, a hormonal workup that included an analysis of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex steroids, and catecholamine was done before surgery, which showed negative findings. The tumour was excised. Pathological findings showed adrenocortical carcinoma, stage pT3N0, with a free surgical margin. After surgery, the patient's health improved.
Right-sided huge retroperitoneal malignancy can mimic a huge hepatocellular carcinoma when located close to the liver. Being supplied by many blood vessels, such tumours can present with early enhancement in the arterial phase and early washout in the venous phase relative to normal liver findings in abdominal CT scans. Because there is biliary tract compression, patients may have increased serum concentrations of liver enzymes and bilirubin. These findings might lead to a misdiagnosis by physicians. This incorrect diagnosis can be avoided by noticing a tiny fat plane between the tumour and liver or kidney, indicating that the lesion is in fact retroperitoneal in origin. This difference allows us to differentiate between these two difficult-to-distinguish entities. In this case, a life-saving surgical procedure could be performed.
output: A fat plane is found between the normal liver and the tumour in abdominal CT scan

A 28-year-old man was transferred to our hospital after he suddenly lost consciousness in the street. He had an initial diagnosis of opioid overdose. Further, because of respiratory depression, hypoxaemia, miosis, loss of consciousness, and an absence of focal neurological signs and symptoms, the patient was given progressively larger doses of naloxone until he regained consciousness and started breathing normally and spontaneously. He said he had been abusing heroin and so because of this, and the clinical presentation, he was transferred to a clinical toxicology ward for further management. During 12 h of observation, the patient had four further episodes of apnoea despite being given further doses of naloxone. He was initially given a bolus of 0·04 mg intravenously, which was titrated up until his breathing improved. At this point his respiration returned to normal, and he continued treatment with two-thirds of the effective bolus dose infused intravenously every hour. His respiration rate was then monitoried regularly.Recurring periods of apnoea, a need for increasingly larger doses of naloxone, and the history of abuse of unknown amounts of heroin concerned us. Was there an alternative explanation for the patient's presentation? We were specifically worried the patient may have been a so-called heroin body-packer, even though he said he was not. A plain abdominal x-ray showed several foreign bodies (figure). A spiral CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without oral contrast further showed multiple, hyperdense, foreign bodies in the distal section of the oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, and colon (figure). The patient was immediately taken to surgery because of signs of gastrointestinal obstruction, the large number of packets seen on the CT scan, the gradual loss of consciousness, and the risk of packets being broken by a nasogastric tube during a whole bowel irrigation. A total of 82 packets containing heroin—including five that the patient vomited up while being transferred to the operating theatre—were retrieved from the stomach and bowels following total gastrotomy. Each packet weighed 20 g—confirmed by a Drug Enforcement Agency officer—and was encased in two condoms. The patient was later arrested by the police after making a full recovery and being discharged from hospital. We do not know the outcome of any legal proceedings involving the patient. However, under Iranian law, it is illegal to possess, transport, and be involved in the trade of narcotics; punishment can be up to 15 years of imprisonment, and in some cases, the offender is sentenced to death.
In cases of heroin overdose, if respiratory depression is not reversed following repeated intravenous bolus doses of naloxone—a total of 10–12 mg of naloxone can be given as intravenous boluses—then it is not recommended to set up an intravenous infusion.
options: Lead-contaminated opium overdose, Toxic megacolon due to methadone overdose, Complications of heroin body-packing, Ileus following lithobezoars

A 6-year-old boy with Ewing's sarcoma presented with generalised skin rash, low grade fever (38°C), and red eyes. Itchiness in the hands and feet preceded the rash. The child received chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide) and blood transfusion 1 week before the onset of symptoms. Examination revealed purplish discoloration of both palms and soles in a glove and socks pattern (figure, A–C). Lesions resembled petechiae over the trunk, hands and feet, and face. Oral mucosa was erythematous with the rash including both pinnae (figure, D). The boy was neutropenic (haemoglobin 11·5 g/dL, total leucocyte count 0·5 × 106/L, and platelet count 20 × 109/L).
The striking glove and socks distribution of the rash prompted the diagnosis of papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvoviral infection. Parvovirus serology showed immunoglobulin M positivity. Skin biopsy revealed lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with red-blood-cell extravasation. The boy was initiated on antibiotics (cefoperazone–sulbactam and amikacin, as per unit guidelines for febrile neutropenia), which were stopped 2 days later because he was afebrile and the blood cultures were sterile. Rash resolved with desquamation over the next 2 weeks. Blood counts also normalised after 1 week.
In children, parvovirus B19 infection usually presents as erythema infectiosum. Although uncommon, infection can manifest itself as PPGSS, which is an acute self-limited dermatosis characterised by fever, acral pruritus, oedema, petechiae, and oral lesions. The distinguishing feature is the symmetric erythema of hands and feet, with sharp margins at wrists and ankles. Other causes of PPGSS include cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus, and measles virus. The disease is mostly self-limited with a benign prognosis.
Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency that needs prompt initiation of antibacterial treatment. Recognition of such a classic manifestation, especially in an immunocompromised host, is essential to avoid aggressive treatment. Unlike patients with erythema infectiosum, individuals with PPGSS are regarded as infectious and should be isolated. Further, immunocompromised children need to be monitored for red-cell aplasia as a manifestation of persistent parvovirus infection. The index child has been well since illness, and completed his chemotherapy in June 2013.
options: Henoch–Schönlein purpura, Transient aplastic crisis, Glomerulonephritis, Myocarditis

A 72-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with sudden onset crampy, generalised abdominal pain. She had a history of peptic ulcer disease, chronic constipation, and heavy smoking. She was tachycardic and febrile, and had generalised peritonism. Her white cell count was 13·6 × 109 cells per L. CT showed pneumoperitoneum in the upper abdomen and pelvic free fluid without oral contrast extravasation (figure A, B). There was faecal loading without features of mechanical obstruction.The patient was thought to have a perforated peptic ulcer and was booked for emergency surgery. Diagnostic laparoscopy, however, revealed faeculent peritonitis and a sigmoid colonic perforation (figure C). Extensive laparoscopic washout, sigmoid colectomy, and colostomy formation were done. Postoperatively, the patient had no major complications. She underwent successful reversal of her stoma 9 months later.
Histopathology assessment showed an 11 mm, full-thickness, rounded antimesenteric defect with no evidence of diverticular disease or a malignant process. The diagnosis was consistent with stercoral perforation. Subsequent colonoscopy confirmed the absence of diverticula and malignancy in the remaining colon and rectum.
Approximately 15% of the population have constipation, although most improve with lifestyle measures and aperients. However, a rare and unusual life-threatening complication of chronic constipation is stercoral perforation. Stercoral perforation is the reported cause of 3·4% of colonic perforations. The pathology is characterised by an antimesenteric, round colonic perforation larger than 10 mm, faecal contamination exuding through the perforation, necrosis, and an inflammatory reaction around the perforation in the absence of tumours, diverticular disease, and trauma. Risk factors for stercoral perforation in patients with chronic constipation include older age (median age 62 years) and smoking. Stercoral perforation has a high mortality of approximately 30–40% and is a devastating sequela of chronic constipation. Many clinicians are sceptical of the diagnosis of stercoral perforation, citing other predisposing bowel pathology, such as diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancy, as the main pathology, with inspissated stool as a disease-modifier. However, this case suggests that stercoral perforation is a true entity independent of other disease processes.

A 61-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 5-day history of sudden-onset, persistent myocloni in his left leg and the left side of his abdomen. Previously, the patient had been fit and well. He reported no recent fever, headache, or trauma.
14 months before admission, the patient had an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated nucleophosmin 1 which resulted in full remission.
On examination, we found the patient generally well; he had painless, rhythmic myocloni, with a frequency of 0·5–1·0 per s, of the proximal left leg and abdomen. The movements were continuous and would not be triggered or suppressed by any specific movements. The patient had no other atypical findings and cognitively was fully alert and conscious.
Laboratory investigations—apart from a previously described macrocytosis—were within typical range.
On day 1 after admission, an MRI of the patient's brain showed multiple cortico-subcortical fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery hyperintense lesions without diffusion restrictions or contrast-enhancement (figure).On day 2 after admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses showed normal cell and protein count; microbial multiplex PCR testing and cytology tests for malignancies were negative.
On day 3, a scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no epileptiform discharges that correlated with the myocloni. Further investigations found no neoplasms.
On day 5, the myocloni extended to the proximal part of the left arm despite the patient being given multiple antiseizure medications.
On day 8 after admission, a biopsy of the brain was done and histopathological analysis of a sample of the biopsy showed T-cell-dominated perivascular lymphocyte infiltrates and endothelial proliferations without evidence of viral infection, demyelination, graft-versus-host disease, or neoplasia.
From day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated; he became disorientated and confused, then drowsy and stuporous; the myocloni continued.
Repeated MRIs, from days 5 to 12 after admission, showed progression of the multiple cortico-subcortical lesions (figure); the EEG showed right-hemispheric temporo-parietal focal slowing independent of the worsening of the patient's condition.
On day 15 after admission, he developed electroclinical super-refractory status epilepticus, which was finally terminated by continuous intravenous thiopental. At this stage autoimmune encephalitis was suspected and immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone, plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulins, and rituximab started; serum and CSF—collected prior to initiation of the treatments—was subsequently found to be positive for GABAA receptor antibodies (serum titre 1:320; normal <1:20; CSF titre 1:1), confirming the diagnosis of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis.
On day 33 and day 185, MRIs showed improvement (figure) with concomitant decreases in serum antibody titres (day 79, 1:20; day 186, <1:20) and serum neurofilament light chain concentrations—day 34, 511·5 pg/mL (99·995 percentile); day 233, 25·4 pg/mL (97·20 percentile).
During the period of hospitalisation, the patient experienced multiple complications, including asystole, which required resuscitation, and critical-illness poly-neuromyopathy. After a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit, the patient was transferred to a neurorehabilitation unit.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient was ambulatory and had mild, residual paresis of his left leg (video); his neurological deficits continued to improve.
Autoantibodies against GABAA receptor cause an encephalitis characterised by seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and movement disorders. Underlying pathogenic mechanisms are, in most cases, unclear; associations between haematological malignancies and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants—as in our case—causing immune dysregulation may indicate possible aetiologies. Studies have reported a range of 9 to 43 months from completion of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant to the development of GABAA receptor encephalitis.
Typical MRI changes, in conjunction with the patient's history and symptoms, should prompt consideration of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis; confirmatory autoantibody results—often available only after a significant length of time—should not delay treatment initiation.
options: Anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis, Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder, Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis

A 60-year old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of a painful, swollen left knee and a fever. She had a medical history of osteoarthritis, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia.On examination she looked unwell; she was tachycardic (heart rate 104 beats per min) and febrile (temperature 39·1°C). She had an effusion on her left knee.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8·1 g/dL, platelet count of 90 × 109 per L and white blood cell count was 5·1 × 109 per L, but with 6% blasts—confirmed on blood smear. 7 months earlier the patient's blood tests had been normal. Analysis of fluid obtained from arthrocentesis was consistent with pseudogout. An infection screen was negative. However, given the fever with functional neutropenia, we decided to commence her on broad spectrum antibiotics.
Bone marrow examination showed 20–25% blasts and morphology consistent with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with myelodysplasia-related changes (figure). Flow cytometry dot plots of the marrow aspirate showed approximately 21% CD34+ and CD117+ myeloblasts (figure). The patient's karyotype was complex—among several abnormalities it included monosomy of chromosome 17 (appendix). Additionally, a pathogenic mutation of the TP53 gene with a variable allele frequency of 64% was detected by next generation DNA sequencing using a 49 gene panel.
Given the patient's comorbidities, her unfit physical state, the complex karyotype, and the TP53 mutation, it was decided, after discussion with her, to try a combination of the hypomethylating agent—azacitidine—and the oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax. The patient developed multiple life-threatening events over subsequent weeks including atrial fibrillation, confusion, and renal failure without tumour lysis. After discussion of options, the family opted for comfort measures and the patient was transferred for care in a hospice and died 6 days later.
Among older patients—especially those with adverse genetic findings—AML is often resistant to chemotherapy and long-term survival rates remain low at 10%. Traditionally, treatment involves intensive chemotherapy followed by allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for fit patients. However, most older AML patients are unfit for curative-intent therapy and receive palliative lower intensity regimens. Oral inhibitors of mutant IDH1, IDH2, and FLT3 proteins—found in approximately half of AML patients—are now approved treatments in some countries. In addition to azacitidine with venetoclax, various other combinations have shown improved survival in subpopulations of older AML patients; none of these strategies, however, have been particularly successful in patients with TP53 mutations (appendix; video).

A 74-year-old woman with a 3-month history of general malaise and loss of appetite was referred to our unit for investigation of hyperviscosity syndrome. The patient had initially attended her local hospital reporting cyanosis and mild oedema of the toes on both her feet. She also had splenomegaly and polyclonal gammopathy: IgG concentration was 3320 mg/dL (typical range 861–1747), IgA was 508 mg/dL (typical range 93–393), and IgM 1648 mg/dL (typical range 50–269). The progressive hyperviscosity of the patient's blood specimens made further testing difficult, hence the referral to our hospital.
On examination she was generally well; neurologically she had no abnormalities, and a visual examination was within normal limits. The patient reported a 3-month history of episodic bleeding from haemorrhoids.
Laboratory investigations showed complement C3 serum concentration of 68 mg/dL (normal range 80–140), CH50 19·5 U/mL (normal range 30–45), and rheumatoid factor 21480 IU/mL (normal <15).
Plasma exchange was initiated, before which the patient tested positive for hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1b. Before and after plasma exchanges, several Ouchterlony double immunodiffusion assays found no precipitation: negative results. Likewise, a skin biopsy showed inconclusive evidence of vasculitis.
However, based on our clinical suspicion of cryoglobulinemia due to HCV, and after consultation with the laboratory department, we did a visual screening test to see if we could find evidence of cryo-precipitation. We showed the patient's serum formed into a gel when cooled to 4°C; the process reversed upon rewarming (figure). Polyclonal IgG and IgM-λ-type M-proteins were detected from the gel using an immunofixation method.We diagnosed hyperviscosity syndrome caused by type II cryoglobulinemia secondary to HCV; treatment with sofosbuvir and velpatasvir achieved a sustained virological response.
3 months later, the patient developed cryoglobulinemia-induced renal impairment; electron microscopy of a sample of a kidney biopsy showed immune complex deposition in the sub mesangial region. Prednisolone therapy was initiated at 40 mg per day and tapered down following improvement of renal function to 5 mg per day.
Hyperviscosity syndrome is a rare manifestation of HCV-related cryoglobulinemia that can cause a wide spectrum of complications, including purpuric eruptions and renal failure. Cryoglobulinemia should still be considered as a differential diagnosis for unexplained hyperviscosity syndrome for the following reasons: firstly, often there is no correlation between the cryoglobulin level and disease severity; secondly, low concentrations of cryoglobulin may form a gel rather than precipitate; and thirdly, the concentration of cryoglobulin in type I and type II cryoglobulinemia is relatively low.
If cryoglobulinemia is suspected clinically, but not shown through typical laboratory investigations, a visual screening exercise looking for evidence of cryo-precipitation with reversible gel formation upon cooling and rewarming of the patient's serum may be helpful.

A 39-year-old woman was transferred to our neurosurgical service following a fall and development of a progressive quadriparesis over the previous 24 h.The patient had a history of uncontrolled type 1 diabetes and chronic pancreatitis associated with alcohol and benzodiazepine dependence.
On examination, we found her to be fully conscious, afebrile, with a low body-mass index (11 kg/m2). She had motor power on the Medical Research Council scale of grade 3 in her left arm and 0 in all other limbs. The patient had a C3 sensory level and all tendon reflexes were absent. She had reduced anal tone and had to be catheterised because of urinary retention. She had no neck stiffness or other signs of meningism.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 31·3 × 109 per L (normal 4·0–10·0) and increased C-reactive protein concentration of 29 mg/L (normal 0–10), serum sodium concentration was 124 mmol/L (normal 133–146), and blood glucose concentration was 31·49 mmol/L (4·0–5·4). We found no ketones in her urine. We corrected the patient's metabolic abnormalities.
CT of the brain and cervical spine showed no abnormalities, but MRI demonstrated a swollen, oedematous spinal cord with T2 hyperintensities from the craniovertebral junction to the conus with patchy enhancement (figure; appendix). T2 sagittal images of the lumbar spine showed a vertical fluid level at the lumbosacral junction: sediment sign (figure).
Shortly after admission, the patient deteriorated: she had respiratory failure and an aspiration pneumonitis requiring endotracheal intubation and prone ventilation. She was started on high dose dexamethasone because the diagnosis was uncertain and the acute swelling of the spinal cord.
The sediment sign on the MRI prompted an urgent lumbar puncture in the prone position—despite her unstable condition. The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was cloudy, contained 1530 white blood cells per mm3 (90% polymorphs and no malignant cells), protein was 11·35 g/L (normal 0·18–0·58), glucose was less than 50% of serum glucose levels and lactate concentration was 12·2 mmol/L. The Gram stain was negative, and cultures grew Streptococcus constellatus.
With respiratory support for 2 weeks and intravenous antibiotics for 6 weeks, the patient made satisfactory clinical improvement: her motor power improved to good functional use on her right side, but she remained hemiparetic on her left. She was then transferred for neurorehabilitation at our National Spinal Injuries Unit. T2-weighted MRI at 3 months showed resolution of the swelling of the spinal cord and disappearance of the sediment sign (appendix).
Extensive spinal cord myelitis is uncommon in bacterial meningitis. The lumbar sediment sign has been described in patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage and occurs because of the layering of altered blood products within the CSF at the lumbosacral junction. It has not been described in meningitis—although a similar layering of debris maybe seen in the occipital horns of patients with ventriculitis due to the combination of proteinaceous and necrotic material within the CSF. We postulate that the mechanism of production of lumbar sedimentation in our case is similar: the vertical fluid level was accounted for by the patient's position in the scanner. In the absence of classic features of meningitis—as in our case—the presence of a lumbar sediment sign raised the suspicion of meningitis, and directed specific investigations and appropriate treatment.
output: Signs and symptoms alone do not provide sufficient information to diagnose meningitis

7 years earlier, she had an episode of left flank pain caused by a stone in her distal left ureter, which was evacuated after insertion of a single-J splint.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; microscopy of a sample of fresh urine sediment showed multiple amorphous ovoid crystals (figure). Laboratory investigations—including full blood count, glucose and lipid metabolism, liver function tests, muscle enzymes, parathyroid and thyroid function tests, and inflammatory and immunological markers—found no abnormalities suggestive of primary or secondary glomerular diseases. Additionally, despite renal impairment, the patient had profound hypouricemia (serum uric acid concentration <0·5 mg/dL; typical range in an adult post-menopausal woman is 3·4–7·0).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed two normal kidneys without nephro-urolithiasis.
Urinary excretion of uric acid was abnormally low (<3 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 443–695); urinary excretion of hypoxanthine was slightly elevated (16 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 7–13); and urinary excretion of xanthine was high (135 mmol/mol creatinine; normal 9–14); indicating a possible diagnosis of either type I or type II xanthinuria. Molecular genetic sequencing found two mutations in the XDH gene on chromosome 2, which encodes for the enzyme xanthine dehydrogenase (OMIM 278300: heterozygous mutations c.3847C>T [p.Arg1283*] and c.3520-69_*3432delinsCAGTCGCT); no mutations were found in the MOCOS gene on chromosome 18, which encodes for molybdenum cofactor sulferase, corroborating the diagnosis of hereditary xanthinuria type I.
The patient was informed of the diagnosis and advised to follow a low-purine diet and drink plenty of fluids; she was counselled about possible genetic testing of her siblings.
At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was clinically well and her renal function was stable.
Hereditary xanthinuria is characterised by high levels of xanthine in the urine; uric acid is much reduced in the serum and urine—compared with gout where an increased concentration of serum urate (hyperuricaemia) is the important risk factor. Two clinically similar forms of xanthinuria are found: type I—our patient—where there is an isolated deficiency of xanthine dehydrogenase, and type II, with a deficiency of both xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase (appendix).
Xanthinuria may occur in molybdenum cofactor sulferase deficiency; type II xanthinuria is caused by a mutation in the MOCOS gene. Excess xanthine can accumulate in the kidneys and other tissues; in the kidneys it may lead to stones and in the muscles, pain and cramping. Apart from a low-purine diet and high fluid intake, which prevent xanthine accumulation, no specific therapies are available for this rare autosomal recessive disorder of purine metabolism. Symptoms may occur at any age, with approximately 50% of patients presenting with urinary tract infections, haematuria, renal colic, acute renal failure, crystalluria, or urolithiasis. Rarely patients’ renal disease may result in failure.

A 69-year-old white woman without risk factors for oral cancer presented at the Plastic Surgery Unit of the University Hospital of Palermo (Palermo, Sicily) in January, 2016, with a fetid and bleeding tumour on the left side of the palate (figure). The mass had developed about 6 months previously and had grown rapidly. The initial suspected diagnosis was squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity. No specific other symptoms were reported and her blood tests were almost normal, with the exception of a non-specific state of malnutrition due to a reduced food intake, and anaemia due to malnutrition and bleeding from the tumour. Blood tests also showed her to be immunocompetent. CT scan showed bone destruction involving the palate.Under local anaesthesic, a biopsy was performed and the histopathological diagnosis, according to the 2016 revision of the WHO classification of lymphoid neoplasms, was Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-positive, B-cell lymphoma, Burkitt's lymphoma subtype (CD20+, CD3–, EBV+, MUM1+ Bcl6–, CD10–,CD30+,CD15–, Ki67 45%).
The patient was transferred to the oncohaematology unit at the hospital to receive treatment with radiotherapy (total dose of 45 Gy given over 4 weeks, administered in a continous course over 4 days per week in doses of 2·5 Gy per fraction) and chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone [CHOP], given in eight cycles for 3 weeks. Despite the biologically aggressive behaviour of the tumour, at 18 months follow-up, the disease seemed to be in remission.
Burkitt's lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with a poor prognosis. This type of lymphoma is rare outside Africa where is endemic. WHO classifies three variants of Burkitt's lymphoma: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated types. The endemic form develops most frequently in young people in Africa (children, adolescents, and young adults less than 40 years of age) and is associated with Epstein–Barr virus infection. It typically involves the mandible, maxilla, and abdomen. The sporadic form has no geographical predilection and develops most often in adults, most commonly presenting as an abdominal mass and rarely presenting in the orofacial region. Only a small subset of non-endemic Burkitt's lymphomas are Epstein–Barr virus positive. The immunodeficiency-related variant usually is associated with HIV infection and rarely involves the orofacial region.
Because Burkitt's lymphoma grows rapidly. timely diagnosis and treatment are important. The physician must be able to recognise this disease, to have an adequate degree of suspicion to consider this option in the differential diagnosis with other tumours or inflammatory diseases, and to understand the steps necessary to treat this aggressive malignancy.
output: Non-Hodgkin B-type lymphoma, Epstein–Barr virus positive, sporadic variety

A 28-year-old man from the rural area of Tamil Nadu attended our specialist hospital, complaining of multiple, copper-coloured patches on his skin, forehead, arms, and the front and back of his torso (figure). On examination he also had bilateral thickening of his ulnar and median nerves, without any functional impairment; multiple slit skin smear tests were positive for acid-fast bacilli in most of the patches on his body. We made a diagnosis of multibacillary, or lepromatous, leprosy, and started the patient on a 12-month course of multidrug therapy (MDT)—rifampicin 600 mg once a month, dapsone 100 mg daily, and clofazimine 300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily. However, within a month, the patient developed raised erythematous lesions over the pre-existing skin patches (figure) as well as general constitutional symptoms including a fever and severe neuritis. A full blood count was normal and serological testing for any additional infections was negative. Biochemical investigations showed abnormal liver function tests (appendix). On the basis of these findings, we made a diagnosis of a severe type 1 leprosy reaction—also known as a reversal reaction—occurring alongside an adverse reaction to dapsone. The patchy, exfoliative dermatitis along with the swollen lips, fever, and hepatitis were key in reaching a diagnosis of an adverse reaction to dapsone. We stopped the MDT regimen, and started the patient on corticosteroids, beginning with a high dose and tapering over subsequent weeks—the hope was that the steroids would help both the adverse reaction to the dapsone and the reversal reaction. At follow-up visits, the patient showed improvement both clinically and biochemically, as indicated by the liver function tests (appendix). We restarted the MDT regimen but this time excluded the dapsone.5 months later the patient again showed signs of a type 1 leprosy reaction. We considered re-starting the dapsone—to see if the patient remained allergic to the drug and because it might have assisted in the treatment of the Mycobacterium leprae—but the patient was unwilling to try this. So he continued the MDT alone—rifampacin and clofazimine—without further treatment with corticosteroids as the neuritis was reasonably controlled by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and regular physiotherapy.
Leprosy has a wide range of presentations, from the lepromatous forms to the borderline forms (borderline-tuberculoid, mid-borderline, and borderline-lepromatous) to the tuberculoid forms. Type 1 or reversal reactions mostly occur in borderline-tuberculoid leprosy with a persistence of cell-mediated immunity. They are diagnosed when raised erythematous patches occur over pre-existing skin lesions in patients undergoing treatment. If the reaction is accompanied by fever, neuritis, or oedema of the hands or feet, it is categorised as a severe reaction and needs treatment with corticosteroids. Dapsone hypersensitivity affects a much smaller—and often unrecognised—population of patients: it is essentially an allergy with clinical features of a fever, skin rashes, mucosal involvement, lymphadenitis, and hepatitis. It carries a mortality of 9·9% and is probably often unrecognised because patients may not have routine blood tests in resource-poor settings. Laboratory findings show an eosinophilia, deranged liver function tests, and, rarely, renal failure. Patients with reversal reactions and hypersensitivity—as in our case—can be managed with the MDT regimen of rifampicin and clofazimine.

input: A 26-year-old woman presented with recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis on all four limbs, deep vein thrombosis involving the lower limbs, fever, a large fungating non-healing ulcer on the left cubital fossa (figure 1A), episodic abdominal pain, and weight loss for the past 4 months. The patient did not complain of oral or genital ulcers, ocular involvement, or altered bowel habits. Her blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg; and her left radial pulse and left brachial pulse in the dorsalis pedis were absent, with carotid bruits heard on both sides. The patient tested negative for antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and inherited thrombophilia. Pathergy and Mantoux tests were negative. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 60 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 91 mg/L. Microbial cultures from the ulcer and blood were negative. CT showed thickening and segmental dilatation of the ascending aorta, aortic arch, descending thoracic and abdominal aorta, and its major branches (figure 1B). Whole body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET showed 18F-FDG avid circumferential wall thickening of the whole aorta and its major branches, without any organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or lung involvement, suggesting active type V Takayasu arteritis. Skin biopsy revealed suppurative necrotising (predominantly neutrophilic) inflammation of the deep dermis (figure 1C), mixed inflammatory infiltrates, secondary vasculitis (lymphocytic), absence of granulomas, and testing for acid-fast bacilli was negative, consistent with a diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum. The patient was started on oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg) with monthly cyclophosphamide pulses (15 mg/kg) for 12 months. A marked improvement in symptoms and complete healing of the skin lesions with some scarring was seen after 6 months of therapy (figure 1D).Pyoderma gangrenosum is an uncommon manifestation of Takayasu arteritis reported in 1–30% of patients in various studies. The treatment of pyoderma consists primarily of corticosteroids and immunosuppressive therapy in severe or refractory cases. Superficial thrombophlebitis and venous thrombosis are also rarely described in Takayasu arteritis. The sites involved include the subclavian vein, jugular vein, and cephalic vein.

A man aged 57 years, who had had herpes zoster 10 years previously, visited our emergency room with a tingling ache in his right lower back. Physical examination revealed neither eruption nor trauma on the body surface. However, an abdominal wall protrusion was observed on his right side, especially while he was standing (figure). Abdominal imaging using contrasted computer tomography did not reveal any abnormalities.Abdominal muscle paralysis was considered as the possible diagnosis and 60 mg loxoprofen, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, was administered for his back pain once daily for 5 days. 5 days after the initial visit, dome-shaped papules with overlying small, dark-coloured vesicles appeared on his trunk and extremities, suggesting disseminated herpes zoster. The patient was treated with 1000 mg oral valacyclovir three times daily for 7 days, along with the same regimen of loxoprofen as already described. The vesicular papules dried up after 5 days and became brown scabs within a week. The protruding abdominal wall flattened within a month, and the patient's lower back pain gradually abated within a couple of months.
Herpes zoster is characterised by the reactivation of the varicella zoster virus, which causes a vesicular rash, typically restricted to a single dermatome. However, some patients develop disseminated herpes zoster; these patients are more likely to be immunosuppressed. It is rare for this condition to occur in an immunocompetent host, as it did in this case.
Post-herpetic abdominal pseudohernia is uncommon, occurring in 2% of patients with herpes zoster. Although pseudohernia should be suspected when a patient develops abdominal paresis coincident with or after a herpetic rash, abdominal paresis can also very rarely precede a rash. Awareness of this clinical condition might help physicians anticipate herpes zoster, allowing prompt treatment.

A 23-year-old man was admitted to our hospital in status epilepticus—he had been having repeated episodes of generalised tonic-clonic seizures without gaining consciousness between them. He was in a wheelchair. He was intubated and the seizures were controlled with midazolam and he was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). On examination his blood pressure (BP) was 220/110 mm Hg, and his heart rate was 120 beats per min. He was given labetalol and his blood pressure lowered.In his medical history, it was noted that he had experienced recurrent episodes of hypertension and tachycardia, intractable epilepsy, psychiatric problems—specifically depression and anorexia nervosa—and episodic abdominal pain for the past 10 years; he was reportedly pain free during the time between relapses. He had been prescribed phenytoin, sodium valproate, and levetiracetam for the seizures—although his level of concordance was unclear. He had been in a wheelchair for some time because of a weakness in his arms and legs which nerve conduction studies showed a pattern consistent with motor axonal polyneuropathy; he had previously been admitted to hospital with pneumonia and respiratory failure, and it had been difficult to wean him off the prolonged ventilation he had required.
Laboratory investigations—including thyroid profile, autoimmune profile, HIV testing, urinary catecholamines and metanephrines were negative (appendix). An electrocardiogram and an echocardiogram were normal apart from the sinus tachycardia. An electroencephalogram showed bursts of alpha waves without any epileptic activity. A CT of the patient's brain was normal, but an MRI showed bilateral asymmetric vasogenic oedema within both occipital and parietal regions—a picture typical of so-called posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (figure).
A Hoesch bedside screening test was positive for urinary porphobilinogen and further testing of a urine sample found a porphobilinogen concentration of 1490 μmol/L (normal <8·8). We therefore made a diagnosis of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) and treated the patient with a high carbohydrate diet, delivered by a nasogastric tube, and a continuous intravenous infusion of 10% dextrose solution.
Within 2 weeks, the patient's symptoms had resolved, and he was extubated and discharged from the ICU fully conscious and with his BP controlled. The anticonvulsants were stopped, and he was started on haematin therapy.
The classic triad of AIP is abdominal pain, psychosis, and neuropathy. Patients may have a tachycardia and seizures will be seen in about 20% of cases. Patients with porphyric neuropathy may be a source of confusion in practice, and the diagnosis—as in our patient—may be delayed. Porphyric neuropathy looks to all intents and purposes like acute Guillain–Barré syndrome. However, the presence of psychological features, a proximal, asymmetric weakness, and electrodiagnostic findings indicative of an axonal polyradiculopathy or neuronopathy point the way to a diagnosis of porphyria (video).

A 31-year-old HIV-positive man presented to the hospital on June 30, 2022, with a vesicular rash (figure A), perianal lesions, swollen inguinal lymph nodes, and arthralgia of the right knee. Under antiretroviral therapy, the HIV viral load was below the limit of detection, and his CD4+ T-cell count was 802 cells per μL. Given the rising number of monkeypox cases in Europe at that time and the patient's history of unprotected sexual contact with a man 1 week before symptom onset, an infection with monkeypox virus was suspected. Specimens from two different skin lesions yielded a positive PCR result (cycle threshold values of 20 and 21) for monkeypox virus. The patient was discharged and self-isolated.11 days later a follow-up examination was scheduled, the rash and lymphadenopathy had completely resolved, but a marked swelling of the right knee was noted (figure B). Arthrocentesis was performed, resulting in aspiration of 60 mL of cloudy synovial fluid. Analysis of the synovial fluid showed a cell count of 16 127 cells per μL with 88·5% mononuclear cells (lymphocytes) and 11·5% neutrophil granulocytes. The synovial fluid PCR yielded a positive result for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 27). Laboratory test results were unremarkable apart from a slightly elevated C-reactive protein of 18 mg/L.
Bacterial cultures and broad-range PCR of synovial fluid, serological testing for rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies and antinuclear antibodies, human leukocyte antigen B27, and PCR for Lyme disease were all negative. A second arthrocentesis was needed 8 days later due to reoccurrence of effusion. PCR of synovial fluid was again positive for monkeypox virus (cycle threshold value of 33), whereas PCR of whole-blood was negative for monkeypox virus. MRI showed synovitis, joint effusion, and a marked oedema of the medial femoral condyle with a subchondral demarcation zone of 1 cm, compatible with the diagnosis of arthritis and osteomyelitis (figure C–E). Treatment with non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory drugs led to improvement of arthralgia and swelling within 3 weeks.
Viruses are common triggers of arthritis, but viral bone infection has only rarely been reported. However, viral osteomyelitis was a typical complication of smallpox. Referred to as osteomyelitis variolosa, it affected 2–5% of children and 0·25–0·50% of all patients infected with smallpox. No cases of monkeypox-related arthritis or osteomyelitis have been described in the literature so far. Considering that variola virus and monkeypox virus are closely related, we believe that monkeypox virus might lead to arthritis and potentially osteomyelitis.
